Name: Inter-table Breathing
What it does (technical): .t + .t { margin-top: 6mm; } — adjacent-sibling selector applies a gap only between consecutive tables; the first table sits flush with content above
How it helps automated designs: One CSS rule auto-spaces every back-to-back table pair without per-instance margin logic
Drawbacks: Wrapping a div between the two tables defeats the selector; 6mm can be tight when both tables carry dense captions
Plain-language explanation: Like the polite gap between two strangers in a bus queue — the rule only fires when there is somebody to leave space from
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Flex-Column Bottom-Pinning
What it does (technical): .page-body { display: flex; flex-direction: column; } with margin-top: auto on the child that should float to the bottom
How it helps automated designs: Footers, signatures and bottom-treatments anchor to the floor of the page regardless of body length, with no absolute positioning math
Drawbacks: Requires a defined container height; Chromium can collapse flex children at page fragmentation unless paired with break-inside: avoid
Plain-language explanation: Like a spring under the bottom shelf of a bookcase — whatever you put on it always ends up touching the floor
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Eyebrow Folding
What it does (technical): Continuation pages drop the big section title and carry a small eyebrow with the section name plus a ' — continued' or ' · cont''d' marker; can be wired via @page rules + string-set or explicit .continuation class
How it helps automated designs: Multi-page sections stay navigable: readers always know which chapter they are in without re-rendering the full hero on every page
Drawbacks: Hardcoded ' — continued' string in many implementations; @page string-set is Chromium-blind so paged-media engines (Prince/WeasyPrint/PagedJS) are required for the elegant path
Plain-language explanation: Like a TV episode title that appears huge in the cold open and then shrinks to a tiny corner tag for the rest of the hour
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, forge + outside research

Name: 66-Character Measure Cap
What it does (technical): p, li { max-width: 66ch; } or column-width: 28em for 2-column print; Bringhurst's ideal of 45-75 characters per line
How it helps automated designs: Caps auto-generated body text to book-like line length without per-document tuning — the highest-leverage single fix
Drawbacks: ch unit varies by font; on already-narrow page bodies the cap is moot
Plain-language explanation: Like a paperback column — short enough that your eye does not have to swing a long tennis return to find the next line

Name: Body Font Floor 16px
What it does (technical): Effective body text must be at least 16px; headers proportionally larger. Enforced as a QA deduction in screenshot-first rubrics
How it helps automated designs: Sets a hard floor that prevents auto-gen pipelines from emitting micro-type that passes code review but fails the back-row read test
Drawbacks: Condensed typefaces at 16px visually read smaller; ''effective'' size requires judgement at the reviewer
Plain-language explanation: If you need a magnifier to read it, it fails — twelve-point looks fine on your laptop and disappears at the back of the room

Name: Body Leading 1.4-1.5
What it does (technical): body { line-height: 1.5; } unitless; display sizes tightened to ~1.1. Bringhurst-codified inverse leading: smaller type wants more leading, larger type wants less
How it helps automated designs: Defaults browsers ship (~1.2) are too tight for long-form; one global rule lifts the document from web-like to book-like
Drawbacks: Looser leading inflates page count; CJK fallback metrics can render 1.5 like 1.8
Plain-language explanation: Row spacing in a parking lot — too tight and cars scrape, too wide and you waste asphalt. 1.5x is the sweet spot for small type

Name: Display Leading Tight
What it does (technical): h1 { line-height: 1.05-1.1 } at display sizes; never apply the body 1.5 globally
How it helps automated designs: Display headlines hold together as a unit instead of floating apart line-by-line, which is the cheapest ''looks designed'' signal
Drawbacks: Tight leading on multi-line headlines risks descender/ascender collisions; needs per-element control
Plain-language explanation: Big drumsticks pack tighter than little ones — large type is already breathing, you do not have to add more air
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa + outside research

Name: Widows And Orphans 3
What it does (technical): p { orphans: 3; widows: 3; } inside @media print — honored by WeasyPrint/Prince/PagedJS/Chromium-print
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates the single-line-at-top-of-page disgrace and lone-first-line-at-bottom embarrassment automatically across the whole document
Drawbacks: Firefox does not implement; aggressive settings can force short pages with whitespace pockets
Plain-language explanation: Like an editor who refuses to let a single line dangle alone at the top of the next page like a guest left at an empty table

Name: Knuth-Plass Paragraph Composition
What it does (technical): text-wrap: pretty (Chrome 117+) for global paragraph optimization, or LaTeX/Prince paragraph composer; treats the whole paragraph as the unit and minimizes ''badness'' across line breaks
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates rivers and the staircase rag that greedy first-fit line-breakers produce — the #1 perceptual tell of machine-generated text
Drawbacks: Slower than greedy; reflow cost on resize; not yet universal in headless Chromium. Chromium's `text-wrap: pretty` only tweaks the last 4 lines of a paragraph — it is NOT a full Knuth-Plass optimizer; WebKit's implementation is closer to the real algorithm.
Plain-language explanation: Greedy line-breakers pack a moving van one box at a time, never reopening. Knuth-Plass packs the whole van once you can see every box

Name: Hyphenation With Limits
What it does (technical): p { hyphens: auto; hyphenate-limit-chars: 6 3 2; -webkit-hyphenate-limit-chars: 6 3 2; } plus lang=''en-US''
How it helps automated designs: Required for justified text to avoid whitespace rivers; the limit values keep two-letter dangling syllables from appearing
Drawbacks: Chromium needs hyphenation dictionaries — minimal Docker images silently no-op; without lang attribute browsers skip entirely
Plain-language explanation: Lets long words break across lines like train cars — limits stop a single-letter caboose from getting stranded

Name: Ragged-Right Default
What it does (technical): body { text-align: left; } — only justify when hyphens: auto actually works and measure is ≥60ch, paired with text-align-last: left
How it helps automated designs: Ragged-right always looks intentional; justified-without-hyphenation produces the gappy ''river'' effect that is the #1 tell of automated layout
Drawbacks: Justified reads as more formal; some clients insist on it
Plain-language explanation: Forcing both edges of the text to be flat is hard — only do it if you also let words break. Otherwise let the right edge be ragged like a flag

Name: Tabular Figures In Numerics
What it does (technical): td.num, .num { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-feature-settings: ''tnum'' 1; } — scoped to tables and numeric cells
How it helps automated designs: Forces every digit to the same width so decimal points and thousands separators line up vertically without per-cell hacks
Drawbacks: Tabular figures are wider than proportional; in body prose they look clunky — scope only to tabular contexts. Some display fonts (Cormorant Garamond) lack tnum — pair with a tabular font for numbers.
Plain-language explanation: By default the number 1 is skinny and 8 is fat, so columns wobble. Tabular figures lock every digit into the same box

Name: Old-Style Figures In Prose
What it does (technical): body { font-feature-settings: ''onum'' 1; } or font-variant-numeric: oldstyle-nums — override with tnum in tables
How it helps automated designs: Numbers stop shouting in body paragraphs because old-style numerals have ascenders and descenders like lowercase letters, blending into the line
Drawbacks: Many sans-serifs lack onum and silently fall back to lining; wrong choice in scientific contexts where number prominence matters
Plain-language explanation: Default numerals are all the same height as capital letters, so ''the 1789 revolution'' looks like ''the 1789 REVOLUTION'' — old-style numbers have tails and bellies that blend in

Name: Real Small Caps For Acronyms
What it does (technical): abbr, .eyebrow { font-variant-caps: small-caps; font-feature-settings: ''smcp'' 1; } — never text-transform: uppercase; font-size: 0.8em
How it helps automated designs: NASA, PDF, OKOA stop hammering the line; section labels and acronyms acquire calm authority because the stroke weight is properly designed
Drawbacks: Most web fonts ship without smcp and synthesize anaemic faux small-caps; PPTX has no concept
Plain-language explanation: Real small caps are designed at the right thickness; faked ones are big letters shrunk down to look stick-thin

Name: Optical Sizing On Variable Fonts
What it does (technical): body { font-optical-sizing: auto; } or manual font-variation-settings: ''opsz'' 11 (body) / ''opsz'' 60 (display)
How it helps automated designs: Variable fonts swap stroke contrast and x-height across sizes; one declaration prevents the brittle look of scaling one master across the full range
Drawbacks: Static fonts ignore the property; some lesser-known variable fonts are mis-tuned
Plain-language explanation: Good fonts have multiple ''outfits'' for different sizes; this setting auto-picks the right one for whatever scale you are at
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Negative Tracking On Display
What it does (technical): h1 { letter-spacing: -0.02em; } scaled -0.01em @24pt to -0.03em @72pt+; positive +0.05-0.10em on all-caps
How it helps automated designs: Fonts are spaced for body sizes; at display sizes gaps look comically wide and uppercase letters jam without breathing room
Drawbacks: Over-tightening collides Tr and fi pairs; CSS will not auto-kern beyond font defaults
Plain-language explanation: Big letters look like they have gaps even when they do not; small caps and uppercase look like they are jammed even when they are not
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Hanging Punctuation
What it does (technical): blockquote, p { hanging-punctuation: first allow-end last; } — Safari/WebKit native; Chromium fallback is negative text-indent: -0.4em
How it helps automated designs: Opening quotes, bullets, and line-end periods stop pulling the optical edge inward; the margin reads straight to the human eye
Drawbacks: Most Puppeteer-based pipelines silently no-op as of 2026; Prince/WeasyPrint partial; mature in InDesign and TeX
Plain-language explanation: A period is shorter than a letter, so when it sits at line-end it looks like the margin has a bite missing — optical alignment pushes the dot outside so the visible edge is the letter

Name: Text-Wrap Balance On Headlines
What it does (technical): h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; } — browser balances headlines so all lines are roughly equal length
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates the ''huge first line, tiny second line'' shape and single-word last-line orphans on display text without per-document tuning
Drawbacks: Chrome caps at 6 balanced lines, Firefox at 10; older Puppeteer Chromium silently ignores; reflow cost
Plain-language explanation: Like a barista who pours two cups from one pitcher so they end up the same height — instead of one full and one half.

Name: Text-Wrap Pretty On Body
What it does (technical): p { text-wrap: pretty; } — Chrome 117+ paragraph-aware line breaker that avoids orphan last words
How it helps automated designs: Auto-eliminates the most common typographic tell (a single dangling last-line word) across all body paragraphs without per-document work
Drawbacks: Slower than the greedy default; not yet universal in headless rendering pipelines
Plain-language explanation: Like a tailor who tucks the last word of a paragraph back into the line above so no single word is left hanging at the bottom.

Name: Modular Type Scale
What it does (technical): Pick one ratio (1.125 Major Second, 1.25 Major Third, 1.333 Fourth, 1.5 Fifth, 1.618 Golden) and one base (16px). All sizes = base × ratio^n via CSS custom properties
How it helps automated designs: Forces all headings, captions, eyebrows and metrics onto a small mathematically related set, eliminating arbitrary ''h2 is 18px because someone typed 18''
Drawbacks: Ratios above ~1.5 produce huge headlines that wreck narrow columns; pure golden-ratio scales jump too fast for dense UI
Plain-language explanation: Every size is one note up the scale from the size below — the eye reads a chord, not a random pile of sizes

Name: Two-Typeface Ceiling
What it does (technical): Define --font-display, --font-body, and optionally --font-mono. Three families is the absolute outside
How it helps automated designs: Auto-pipelines mixing 5+ fonts always look like Word 2008; a 2-family rule enforced at the variable layer prevents drift
Drawbacks: Tight budget gives up display effects unless the family ships display weights
Plain-language explanation: Pick one fancy headline font, one plain reading font, and stop — like a band with a singer and a guitarist, not seven of each
Source: Inside: design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Mono-Label Eyebrow
What it does (technical): Section labels use IBM Plex Mono at 10-12px, weight 600, letter-spacing 0.04-0.25em, uppercase, format '01 — Section Name' with em dash
How it helps automated designs: Creates a consistent ''administrative text'' tier across all templates; readers parse mono labels as metadata vs body prose
Drawbacks: IBM Plex Mono is not a system font — the fallback (Courier New) destroys the aesthetic; long monospace labels overflow narrow containers
Plain-language explanation: Like the tiny gray EXHIBIT A stamp on legal documents — always the same typeface and size, so you can scan a 300-page binder and instantly know what you are looking at
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Cormorant Garamond Display Only
What it does (technical): Reserve Cormorant Garamond (or any display serif) for hero h1, section titles, pull quotes, and data hero numbers; IBM Plex Sans handles all body and card titles
How it helps automated designs: Prevents ''typeface promiscuity'' — the common AI-generated failure where headline fonts bleed into body paragraphs and destroy readability
Drawbacks: Constraining the display face to display-only means a maximum of two type personalities; pull-quote citations may want an intermediate treatment
Plain-language explanation: Like a law firm that uses its elegant script only on the letterhead and signature block, never in the legal text
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Sentence-Case Body Text
What it does (technical): Body, bullets, captions in sentence case. ALL CAPS reserved for eyebrows ≤4 words, letter-spaced ≥0.04em
How it helps automated designs: Lowercase shapes are more distinct so the eye reads them ~10-13% faster; readers over 55 are 29% more likely to misread ALL-CAPS
Drawbacks: Some brand systems mandate caps for headers — needs an opt-out
Plain-language explanation: Words have shapes; hello and HELLO have different silhouettes — lowercase shapes are more distinct so your eye reads them faster
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Italics For Emphasis Only
What it does (technical): Reserve italics for single-token emphasis, foreign terms, and titles of works; renderer strips stray italics from extracted text
How it helps automated designs: Pass-through italics from PDF/DOCX extraction becomes noise and renders intentional emphasis invisible
Drawbacks: Editorial styles that italicize quotes break under this rule
Plain-language explanation: If everyone whispers, no one can be heard whispering — italics only work as emphasis if they are rare

Name: Smart Punctuation Preprocessing
What it does (technical): <html lang=''en-US''> plus smartypants pass: straight quotes to curly, -- to em-dash, lone - to en-dash for ranges
How it helps automated designs: Straight quotes and double-hyphens are the #1 typographic tell of Markdown origin; lang attribute also gates hyphenation and line-break per locale
Drawbacks: Code blocks must be excluded; other locales use different quote shapes
Plain-language explanation: Real books use curly quotes and em-dashes — tell the renderer the language and run a smart-punctuation pass before publishing

Name: Non-Breaking Space Heuristics
What it does (technical): Preprocessor inserts   between number+unit (12 mm), title+name (Dr. Smith), and between the last two words of every heading
How it helps automated designs: Forces typographically correct word groupings; last-two-words trick is a renderer-agnostic anti-widow that works without text-wrap: pretty
Drawbacks: Over-zealous injection prevents legitimate breaks and overflows narrow columns
Plain-language explanation: A sticky space tells the renderer ''do not break here'' — between number and unit, or between the last two words of a headline

Name: Penguin Spaced En-Dash
What it does (technical): Replace — with  –  or  –  at renderer level — choose per house style (Penguin UK vs Chicago US)
How it helps automated designs: Avoids the wall-of-dashes look LLM output produces with default em-dashes; spaced en-dash reads calmer in justified text and gives the H&J engine cleaner break points
Drawbacks: Inconsistent with Chicago Manual; jarring for US readers used to closed em-dashes
Plain-language explanation: Americans write ''paused—then continued'' with no spaces; British/Penguin style is ''paused – then continued'' with smaller dash and spaces — the Penguin version is calmer in long paragraphs

Name: Hot-Metal Paragraph Break
What it does (technical): Either p { text-indent: 1.5em; margin: 0 } (book style) OR p { margin: 0 0 1em; text-indent: 0 } (modern/web) — never both
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the ''indented AND space-after'' double-mark that LLM-to-Markdown-to-PDF pipelines produce, where every paragraph looks like a fresh section
Drawbacks: Indent-only fails on first paragraphs after a heading; space-only consumes more vertical room
Plain-language explanation: A paragraph break can be marked by indent OR space — doing both is wasteful and reads as amateur

Name: Drop Cap At Chapter Start
What it does (technical): ::first-letter { initial-letter: 3 2; -webkit-initial-letter: 3 2 } — size in lines + sink; usually paired with small-caps on first 3-5 words
How it helps automated designs: Chapter openings get visual gravity automatically; the convention itself signals ''this is a book, not a report''
Drawbacks: Safari/WebKit only; Chromium does not ship `initial-letter` as of 2026 — needs a manual `float: left` + sized first-letter fallback for Chrome/Puppeteer pipelines. Punctuation-led paragraphs drop the wrong character. Older WeasyPrint/mPDF/Prince need the float-left fallback too.
Plain-language explanation: That oversized first letter at chapter start — a 1600-year-old cue that says ''the story starts here''

Name: Microtype Glyph Protrusion
What it does (technical): pdfTeX \\microtypecontext{protrusion=...,expansion=...} or InDesign Glyph Scaling 98%-102% + Optical Margin Alignment; CSS has no native equivalent
How it helps automated designs: Justified text loses its lake-of-white rivers; the right edge looks straight without obvious stretched word-spaces
Drawbacks: Scaling above 2% distorts letter shapes; protrusion changes the geometric measure for designers anchored to a fixed grid
Plain-language explanation: Pretend each glyph is rubber — stretch the wide ones 1% and pull the punctuation slightly off the edge, and the eye sees a perfect margin without noticing

Name: Italic Last Word Heuristic
What it does (technical): For titles >2 words: split as (words[:-1], words[-1]) and italicize the last word only
How it helps automated designs: Arbitrary user titles get a Cormorant italic treatment without manual markup; last word usually carries noun-weight in title-case strings
Drawbacks: Breaks for verb-first or stop-word-ending titles; acronyms italicize wrong
Plain-language explanation: Like an editor who always italicizes the last word of a headline for rhythm — consistent even when occasionally imperfect

Name: Lobotomized Owl Selector
What it does (technical): .flow > * + * { margin-top: var(--flow-space, 1.5rem); } — applies spacing only between siblings, never on first/last child
How it helps automated designs: Self-correcting: when the generator inserts or omits blocks, top/bottom edges stay flush. Eliminates a whole class of double-margin and missing-bottom-gap bugs
Drawbacks: Universal selector specificity quirks; inside flex/grid, gap is preferable
Plain-language explanation: Spacers go between the books on a shelf, not at the ends — so the row always starts flush against the wall

Name: WCAG AA Contrast Floor
What it does (technical): Compute relative luminance per WCAG; enforce ≥4.5:1 for text below 18pt regular / 14pt bold, ≥3:1 for larger; build-time CI check
How it helps automated designs: Single deterministic pass/fail; wires into the pipeline to block palette mutations that quietly break readability
Drawbacks: Luminance-only — ignores hue perception; pale-yellow on white passes 3:1 but is unreadable
Plain-language explanation: A noise floor — the foreground text must be N decibels louder than the background, measured the same way every time
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa + outside research

Name: WCAG AAA Contrast (Institutional)
What it does (technical): Same algorithm as AA, threshold 7:1 body / 4.5:1 large; apply selectively to long-form reading surfaces
How it helps automated designs: Right level for institutional documents where boss-criticism on a cold first look matters
Drawbacks: Forces near-black-on-white only; washes out warm-cream OKOA-style surfaces
Plain-language explanation: AA is 'I can read this on my phone outside.' AAA is 'I can read this from across the room with sunglasses on.'

Name: APCA Perceptual Contrast
What it does (technical): Compute Lc in 0–±106 range; targets Lc 75 body, Lc 60 large, Lc 90 small/thin; polarity-aware
How it helps automated designs: Reflects human perception; penalizes pale-yellow-on-white that WCAG 2.x passes and rewards thoughtful dark-mode pairings
Drawbacks: Not yet normative (WCAG 3 draft); two scoring systems coexist
Plain-language explanation: WCAG 2 measures the gap between two colors; APCA measures whether you can actually read across the gap

Name: 60-30-10 Palette Distribution
What it does (technical): Page area: ~60% dominant neutral, ~30% secondary, ~10% accent — pre-bake into templates
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the ''Christmas tree'' output that LLMs produce when they pick colors per element
Drawbacks: Heuristic; doesn't formalize which colors are which, so easy to game
Plain-language explanation: A room — walls 60%, furniture 30%, throw pillows 10% — reverse the proportions and the room shouts

Name: One-Accent Rule
What it does (technical): Exactly one hue family marked role: accent; generator forbids more than one chroma >0.12 (OKLCH) on a single composition
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates LLM ''decoration'' with extra brand colors; produces editorial restraint by default
Drawbacks: Bad for dashboards or charts that need categorical encoding via color
Plain-language explanation: A red tie on a navy suit is sharp — two red ties is a costume

Name: One Shout Per Slide
What it does (technical): Per slide or page: exactly one accent color AND at most one out-sized element (headline number or hero image); everything else lives in a flat tonal range
How it helps automated designs: LLMs reach for emphasis (bold, color, size) whenever uncertain — producing pages where six things scream. ''One shout'' forces deterministic priority
Drawbacks: Looks austere; clients who paid sometimes want to see more ''design effort''
Plain-language explanation: In a quiet room one voice carries; in a loud room nobody hears anyone — color and size are voices, so only let one of them speak per page

Name: OKLCH For Palette Generation
What it does (technical): Generate tonal ramps with fixed H + C, stepped L: oklch(L 0.12 250) where L cycles 0.98, 0.92, ..., 0.10
How it helps automated designs: Equal numeric steps look equal; no per-hue manual tuning, one function builds an entire 11-step ramp
Drawbacks: Gamut clipping at high chroma (blues/purples on sRGB); needs in-gamut() clamp pass
Plain-language explanation: HSL is a map where one inch equals one mile in some regions and one mile equals four inches elsewhere — OKLCH is drawn to scale

Name: Tonal Palette Ramps 50-950
What it does (technical): 11-step ramp per hue family (Material 3 / Tailwind style); map semantic tokens to indices, not to hex values
How it helps automated designs: Decouples which shade from which role; a rebrand swaps one hue and all surfaces re-derive automatically
Drawbacks: Index does not equal contrast — still need per-pair contrast check
Plain-language explanation: A paint-chip card with 11 shades of the same color — always grab from the same card so the document stays in one family

Name: Tinted Warm Neutrals Over Pure Gray
What it does (technical): Replace #808080 with hue-tinted neutrals: oklch(0.5 0.01 60) (warm) or oklch(0.5 0.01 240) (cool)
How it helps automated designs: Pure grays render ''dead'' in print and on warm LCDs; tinted neutrals feel intentional and brand-coherent
Drawbacks: A wrong-direction tint reads worse than pure gray
Plain-language explanation: Studio lights are never pure white — they are 3200K or 5600K. Same with neutrals — give them a temperature

Name: Near-Black Instead Of Pure Black
What it does (technical): Use oklch(0.18 0.02 250), #1a1a1a, or #111827 for body text; reserve pure #000 only for ink/print plates
How it helps automated designs: Pure black on warm white looks harsh and clipped; near-black reduces eye-strain and inherits palette temperature
Drawbacks: On low-quality screens or e-paper, near-black can look muddy
Plain-language explanation: Black coffee versus espresso with a single drop of milk — same intent, less harsh

Name: Off-White Surface Instead Of Pure White
What it does (technical): Use oklch(0.985 0.005 80), #fafaf7, or #f9f7f2 for body surfaces; reserve pure #fff for elevated cards only
How it helps automated designs: Cuts screen glare, lets the one accent pop without max-contrast harshness, and reads as ''editorial''
Drawbacks: Off-white can look dirty in print if not deliberately specified
Plain-language explanation: Book paper isn't bleached white — it is warm cream because the eye glides over it without fighting glare
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Semantic Color Indirection
What it does (technical): Two-tier system: Tier 1 raw palette as CSS custom properties (--sage-80, --coral); Tier 2 semantic intent (primary text, accent, on-success). NEVER use Tier 1 directly
How it helps automated designs: Prevents agents from making ad-hoc color choices; eliminates the most common contrast failures from guessing
Drawbacks: Semantic table is often prose/markdown rather than concrete utility classes, leaving room for misapplication
Plain-language explanation: Like paint-by-numbers — instead of choosing from 100 colors you are told ''sky areas use color 7'' and you can't paint the sky red

Name: Signal Color Four-State Vocabulary
What it does (technical): Define exactly four semantic states each with a text/border color and a light surface background: caution (amber on cream), pass (green on mint), risk (deep red), info (slate on pale blue)
How it helps automated designs: Creates a consistent visual language for alerts, notes, callouts and risk boxes — every warning is drawn from the same four-color vocabulary
Drawbacks: Caution amber on cream surface may have insufficient WCAG AA contrast; cultural mismatch (red is lucky in CN)
Plain-language explanation: A traffic-light vocabulary baked into the template — the designer establishes four ''alert'' colors once and every box pulls from the same set
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa + outside research

Name: Color-Blind Safe Categorical Palette
What it does (technical): Default qualitative palette = Okabe-Ito 8-color: #000000, #E69F00, #56B4E9, #009E73, #F0E442, #0072B2, #D55E00, #CC79A7
How it helps automated designs: ~8% of men have deuteranopia/protanopia; ships correct-by-construction without per-document review
Drawbacks: Okabe-Ito looks slightly ''scientific'' — not always brand-on for marketing
Plain-language explanation: Wheelchair ramps at the front door — everyone walks in, nobody has to ask

Name: CMYK-Safe Print Clamp
What it does (technical): Clamp output palette to gamut-reachable values (fogra39 or swop) and avoid pure-sRGB neons; keep total ink coverage <300%
How it helps automated designs: Print PDF output will not surprise the user with washed-out greens or muddy blues
Drawbacks: Shrinks the designer palette substantially
Plain-language explanation: Your monitor can shout colors a printer can only whisper — clamp before sending to press

Name: Diverging Palettes Centered On Zero
What it does (technical): For diverging scales explicitly set midpoint = 0 (or = median); auto-detect from data — if min < 0 < max, force diverging
How it helps automated designs: Auto-correct chart family choice from data shape; never reuse sequential for signed data
Drawbacks: Mid-tone neutral can dominate when data is heavily skewed
Plain-language explanation: Profit and loss share an axis only if zero is the visible pivot — otherwise the chart lies about which is which

Name: Hero Color Routing By Doc Type
What it does (technical): Prescriptive map: master architecture → sage, loan origination → coral, due-diligence → navy, security/risk → ink, executive → sage with photo. Mechanical lookup, no aesthetic judgement
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates color choice entirely for hero backgrounds — the agent identifies the document type and reads the correct color from a table
Drawbacks: Documents spanning multiple types (an exec summary of a security architecture) have no rule for the conflict; bakes in OKOA-specific associations
Plain-language explanation: Like a hospital color-coding system where every department has a specific scrub color — staff don't decide what to wear, the role decides

Name: Section Background Alternation
What it does (technical): Never place two same-background sections adjacent. Alternate default neutral → white → default → dark-color → default → ink → closing. Place colored sections at narrative inflection points
How it helps automated designs: Forces visual rhythm into the document automatically; gives readers perceptual landmarks without designing each transition
Drawbacks: Inflection-point placement is judgment-dependent, not mechanical
Plain-language explanation: Like a restaurant menu where appetizers, mains, and desserts alternate visual weight — structure creates navigation cues without explicit labels

Name: Light-Dark Token Pairing
What it does (technical): :root (light) and :root[data-theme=''dark''] paired token definitions; or CSS light-dark() function for inline pairing
How it helps automated designs: Single source-of-truth for theming; one template renders both modes from the same source
Drawbacks: PDF rendering pipelines often ignore prefers-color-scheme — need explicit mode selection
Plain-language explanation: A double-sided menu — same dishes, different lighting on each side
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Carbon 16-Column Grid
What it does (technical): display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(16, 1fr); column-gap: 32px; — three gutter modes: wide 32px, narrow 16px, condensed 1px
How it helps automated designs: 16 columns divides cleanly into 1/2/4/8 so every common card layout has integer column spans; lets an LLM emit grid-column: span 8 without computing pixel widths
Drawbacks: Generous for letter-size print; sub-column rounding errors at non-power-of-2 spans (span 3 of 16)
Plain-language explanation: Like a bookshelf with 16 evenly-spaced slots — any item you put on it lines up because you can only choose slot-edges

Name: Bootstrap 12-Column Grid
What it does (technical): display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr); gap: 24px; — 12 factors as 2, 3, 4, 6
How it helps automated designs: Natively supports halves, thirds, quarters and sixths — much easier than 16 if the content model includes triplets
Drawbacks: Halves and quarters share a column boundary; eighths are impossible
Plain-language explanation: A clock face — 12 hours subdivides cleanly into halves, thirds, and quarters, but never into eighths
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: 8pt Spacing With 4pt Type Sub-Grid
What it does (technical): All margin, padding, gap, and box dimensions are multiples of 8px; typography line-heights and cap-height adjustments use the finer 4pt sub-grid
How it helps automated designs: Reduces the spacing-token vocabulary from a continuum to ~6 named values; catches drift like 15px or 13px against the 16px rhythm
Drawbacks: Forces rounding at the edges of clamp() ranges; the 4 vs 8 distinction is easy to confuse in code review
Plain-language explanation: Like LEGO bricks — every piece snaps to the same stud spacing so anything you build fits together cleanly

Name: Grid-Template-Areas Named Slots
What it does (technical): .slide { display: grid; grid-template-areas: ''eyebrow eyebrow'' ''kicker body'' ''footer footer''; } and .eyebrow { grid-area: eyebrow }
How it helps automated designs: Decouples content semantics from coordinates — an LLM emits content keyed by area name and never computes pixel positions
Drawbacks: Each row must declare all columns (no sparse syntax); rectangular regions only — no L-shapes
Plain-language explanation: ASCII art for layout — you literally draw the page in your CSS and content slots into the named cells
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: CSS Subgrid For Card Alignment
What it does (technical): .card { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; } so sibling cards share row tracks
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates the ''card heights don't match'' failure in generated portfolio grids and KPI strips without fixed heights or JS
Drawbacks: Padding on the subgrid container shifts tracks and breaks alignment; not yet supported in older Puppeteer Chromium
Plain-language explanation: Like a choir — every singer follows the same conductor so the same beat lands across cards no matter who is singing

Name: Aspect-Ratio For Image Slots
What it does (technical): .img-slot { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%; } pre-reserves layout space before the image loads; pair with object-fit: cover
How it helps automated designs: Guarantees deterministic page totals — generator estimates how many photo-cards fit before network fetches; CLS goes to zero
Drawbacks: At least one dimension must be auto for the rule to apply; in print, intrinsic ratio still wins if both dimensions are explicit
Plain-language explanation: Like a picture frame hung on the wall — the frame is up first and whatever photo you slide in gets cropped to fit
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Clamp() Fluid Typography
What it does (technical): font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 0.5vw, 1.5rem); padding: clamp(16px, 4vw, 48px) — min, preferred, max
How it helps automated designs: Removes the need to emit media queries for each breakpoint; one declaration produces a continuous responsive curve
Drawbacks: For paged-media output viewport units are meaningless — clamp resolves to the preferred value at print time; print pipelines should pre-compute
Plain-language explanation: Like a thermostat with min/max bounds — the room temperature drifts with weather but never goes below 18 or above 24

Name: Manuscript Grid For Long Prose
What it does (technical): One column, wide margins (≥1.25in / 32mm outer, ≥1in / 25mm inner); measure 60-75 characters per line, max-width: 65ch; margin-inline: auto
How it helps automated designs: For memos, legal opinions, narrative reports a single-column generator produces the most legible result — sometimes skipping the grid is the correct technical choice
Drawbacks: Cannot host data tables, charts, or marginalia without breaking out; visually boring at glance — wrong for marketing decks
Plain-language explanation: A book page — one column, fat margins for your thumbs, and a comfortable line length for your eye

Name: Five Elements Max Per Page
What it does (technical): Hard-cap top-level children per slide/page: ≤5 distinct visual objects (headline, supporting line, ≤3 evidence blocks); enforce at YAML/JSON ingest time
How it helps automated designs: Self-policing complexity; prevents the ''kitchen sink'' slide LLMs produce when given verbose source material — forces consolidation upstream
Drawbacks: Data-dense audiences (finance, IC decks) sometimes need 8-12 elements; cap must be slide-class-aware
Plain-language explanation: Like a five-item dinner plate — beyond that the dish becomes a buffet and nobody knows what to taste first

Name: Four Working-Memory Chunks
What it does (technical): Max 4 ± 1 distinct visual items in the body of any single composition; groups of three KPIs become one ''metric grid'' chunk
How it helps automated designs: Caps the YAML-to-render explosion when the LLM extracts 9 facts and dumps all 9; respects short-term memory limits
Drawbacks: Loses the dense executive-summary slide some audiences expect (boards, scientific posters)
Plain-language explanation: Short-term memory is a four-slot tray — set out seven dishes and the audience picks four and forgets three

Name: Rule Of Thirds Focal Placement
What it does (technical): Divide the canvas into 9 cells (3×3); place the focal point on one of the four interior intersections. CSS: object-position: 33% 33% or 66% 33%
How it helps automated designs: Cheap deterministic substitute for taste — a generator placing a portrait should default to upper-right third with caption lower-left, never centered
Drawbacks: Wrong for symmetrical compositions (Bauhaus dead-center); heuristic, not a rule — overrides itself when the subject has a strong horizon
Plain-language explanation: Tic-tac-toe board over the photo — drop your subject on a cross-mark, not the middle square

Name: Golden Ratio Two-Column Split
What it does (technical): Two-column layout: main 61.8%, sidebar 38.2%; CSS: grid-template-columns: 1.618fr 1fr
How it helps automated designs: A single literal value (1.618) replaces a judgment call; never produces the awkward 60/40 or 70/30 split that looks computed
Drawbacks: Folk-overclaimed — many ''golden'' layouts test no better than thirds; don't apply blindly to grids
Plain-language explanation: A waltz beat — strong, weaker, weaker — 61.8 vs 38.2 feels like the larger leads the smaller
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: F-Pattern Vs Z-Pattern Templates
What it does (technical): Content-heavy pages: headline top-left, summary below, key bullets on left margin (F-pattern, Nielsen 2006). Sparse hero pages: headline top-left, hero top-right, CTA bottom-right (Z-pattern). Pick template based on word count
How it helps automated designs: Lets the generator pick a template from a measured content property (word count >150 = F, ≤150 = Z) and removes a recurring ''wrong template'' failure
Drawbacks: RTL languages reverse both; tablet/mobile collapses Z to a vertical stack, losing the pattern
Plain-language explanation: F-pattern is reading a newspaper column; Z-pattern is reading a postcard
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Müller-Brockmann Modular Grid
What it does (technical): Define both modules (rectangular cells = one text-line × one column) and a baseline grid; every block snaps to N modules wide × M modules tall
How it helps automated designs: Two-axis snapping — vertical rhythm and horizontal column structure speak the same vocabulary, so headlines, images and captions stack predictably
Drawbacks: Requires the text-line and column widths to be pre-set; dynamic content overflowing a module needs explicit span rules or truncation
Plain-language explanation: Graph paper for designers — both axes are ruled so you can only place rectangles on integer coordinates

Name: Asymmetric Swiss Layout
What it does (technical): Place dominant elements at column 1 or column 8 of a 16-column grid (not centered); pair with generous left or right whitespace
How it helps automated designs: Auto-generated decks/reports escape the ''centered title, centered subtitle, centered logo'' cliché; asymmetry tells the eye where to start
Drawbacks: Easy to do wrong (off-balance without purpose looks broken); slide aspect ratios fight asymmetric grids
Plain-language explanation: Don't center everything — put the headline on the left edge and let the right two-thirds be empty. The page balances because empty space has weight

Name: Break Grid Once Per Page
What it does (technical): Default: every element snaps to a column/row line. Exception: one hero element per page may span columns asymmetrically (grid-column: 2 / -2; transform: translateX(-12mm))
How it helps automated designs: Allows expressive variation without surrendering consistency — every-slide-on-grid plus one off-grid hero feels intentional
Drawbacks: Easy to over-use; requires a ''breaker budget'' in generator state (max 1 per page, max 3 per 20-page deck)
Plain-language explanation: Wear a suit, add one statement piece — not ten

Name: Van De Graaf Asymmetric Margins
What it does (technical): @page :left { margin: 1.25in 1in 2in 1.5in } @page :right { margin: 1.25in 1.5in 2in 1in } — Van de Graaf or Fibonacci proportions, outer > inner, bottom > top
How it helps automated designs: Auto-generated PDFs stop looking like Word docs with uniform 1in margins; the textblock sits where the eye recognizes from 500 years of book design
Drawbacks: Wastes paper (≥30% margin); generates a bottom margin many modern readers find ''old-fashioned''
Plain-language explanation: A photo frame is wider at the bottom because the eye perceives a centered picture as slightly low — book pages do the same

Name: Outer Margin Exceeds Gutter
What it does (technical): Outer (page) padding ≥1.5× column gutter — typically page padding 32-48mm and column gutter 16-24mm
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the ''wall of text at page edge'' look and makes pages feel composed
Drawbacks: Sacrifices density
Plain-language explanation: A gallery picture has more wall around it than between it and the next picture

Name: Section Inner Offset Centering
What it does (technical): At desktop: section content lives in 14 of 16 grid columns with a 1-column offset on each side (col-offset-lg-1); creates automatic horizontal margins
How it helps automated designs: Creates automatic breathing-room margins at the section level so the agent never manages horizontal padding manually
Drawbacks: At exactly the lg breakpoint the 1-column offset is only ~24px, which can feel tight at narrower widths
Plain-language explanation: Like a book's consistent side margins — every page automatically has the same gutters without the typesetter measuring each one

Name: Narrative Reading Column
What it does (technical): .narrative spans 8 of 16 columns with a 4-column left offset, centering a 720-800px reading column at ~65-75 characters per line
How it helps automated designs: Enforces optimal reading line length automatically; the agent just puts prose in .narrative and the grid handles centering and width-capping
Drawbacks: At very wide viewports the offset of 4 cols makes the narrative slightly left-biased relative to true center
Plain-language explanation: Like newspaper column widths — a broadsheet doesn't run text full-page-width because it would be unreadable
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Baseline Grid In CSS
What it does (technical): All line-height values are multiples of 4px: 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48. Body 16/24; H1 48/56, H2 32/40, H3 24/32; in python-pptx paragraph.line_spacing = Pt(24)
How it helps automated designs: Cross-element vertical rhythm — when a generator intermixes headings, body and pull-quotes, every baseline still lands on a 4px gridline so adjacent blocks visually connect
Drawbacks: True baseline snapping (text baselines, not box edges) is not natively supported in CSS — only the box-rhythm approximation; mixed font-family drifts
Plain-language explanation: Music notation — every note sits on a staff line, and even half-notes and rests fit the rhythm

Name: Negative Space 30% Budget
What it does (technical): Reserve ≥30% of every page or slide as un-marked whitespace; enforce by computing pixel-coverage of content boxes against canvas and rejecting layouts above 70% saturation
How it helps automated designs: Forces the generator to cut content (not compress whitespace) when faced with overflow; saves the document from looking like a 1990s newsletter
Drawbacks: Quantifying ''air'' is fuzzy — pixel-coverage misses visual density of text vs solid blocks
Plain-language explanation: Empty space on a luxury menu says ''we don't need to fill this — we're confident''; a coupon flyer fills every inch because it has to fight for attention

Name: Vertical Fill 70-90%
What it does (technical): Page-fill window — content fills 70%-90% of vertical space; QA deducts for pages below 70% (looks unfinished) or above 90% (cramped/clipping)
How it helps automated designs: Catches both overflowing pages and underbuilt pages; keeps generated layouts in the ''finished document'' appearance band
Drawbacks: Not appropriate for deliberately sparse pages (full-bleed image covers, dividers) — page-type modifier can soften
Plain-language explanation: A page that is 65% full looks like it is missing content; a page that is 95% full looks cramped — stay in the band

Name: Chapter Drop Whitespace
What it does (technical): .chapter > h1 { margin-top: 2in } or @page:first { margin-top: 3in } — 50-75mm drop before chapter title
How it helps automated designs: Forces editorial breathing on every h1 without per-chapter tuning
Drawbacks: Wasteful on short documents
Plain-language explanation: Before a speaker walks on stage, the lights dim and the room quiets — chapter openers do the same on the page

Name: Density Gradient Around Headings
What it does (technical): h1 { margin-bottom: 3rem } h2 { margin-bottom: 2rem } p + p { margin-top: 0.75rem } — more space near titles, less near body
How it helps automated designs: Generator classifies by heading level and the gradient happens automatically — important things get repeated with pauses, body runs fast
Drawbacks: Can feel front-loaded on very short sections
Plain-language explanation: Important announcements get repeated with pauses; small talk runs fast — let your spacing reflect that
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Gap Over Margin Inside Containers
What it does (technical): display: flex; gap: 24px — container-applied, doesn't pollute last child, doesn't collapse, wrapping rows respect the gap
How it helps automated designs: No first/last sentinel logic; wrapping rows respect gap automatically
Drawbacks: No effect outside flex/grid/multicol contexts
Plain-language explanation: Like telling the host of a dinner party how much elbow room each guest needs — instead of pinning a note on each guest's lapel.

Name: Margin Between Padding Within
What it does (technical): Use margin to separate siblings, padding for internal breathing; never mix them on the same element
How it helps automated designs: Avoids double-spacing and ''child margin escapes parent'' margin-collapse bugs
Drawbacks: Requires teaching the templater the distinction
Plain-language explanation: Padding is the cushion stuffing inside a chair; margin is the gap between two chairs — they do different jobs
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, forge + outside research

Name: Block Formatting Context Containers
What it does (technical): display: flow-root (or overflow: hidden, display: flex) on containers whose children's margins must stay inside
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates ''where did my margin go?'' bugs around sections with background-color or borders
Drawbacks: flow-root is 2020+; overflow:hidden clips decoration
Plain-language explanation: Build a fence around the yard so the dog stops escaping into the neighbor's lawn

Name: Card Padding Exceeds Card Gap
What it does (technical): .card { padding: 24px } .grid { gap: 16px } — inside breathing exceeds outside breathing
How it helps automated designs: Card contents feel contained rather than pressed against the edge
Drawbacks: Eats density on small cards
Plain-language explanation: Each card is a room — walls thicker than the corridor that runs between rooms

Name: Cluster Two-Tier Spacing
What it does (technical): .cluster + .cluster { margin-top: 3rem } with tight flow-space-sm inside; two-tier scale for inter- vs intra-group
How it helps automated designs: Maps directly to semantic chunks; reader sees hierarchy without explicit headings
Drawbacks: Requires semantic markup from the generator
Plain-language explanation: Friends at a party stand in tight knots with empty floor between them — the empty floor does the introducing

Name: Heavy Element Optical Breathing
What it does (technical): .heavy + * { margin-top: calc(var(--flow-space) * 1.15) } — bold weight, large display, dark blocks, and photos get +10-20% over mechanical value
How it helps automated designs: Single multiplier corrects optical imbalance without redoing the grid
Drawbacks: ''Heavy'' is hard to detect automatically — requires a class or attribute
Plain-language explanation: A heavy person on a seesaw sits closer to the middle to balance the lighter person on the other end
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, forge + outside research

Name: Trailing Margin Neutralizer
What it does (technical): .flow > *:last-child { margin-bottom: 0 } — or use the owl selector which only applies top-margins
How it helps automated designs: Prevents blank trailing pages from margins that ''escape'' the last child
Drawbacks: Doesn't fix margin collapse across BFC boundaries
Plain-language explanation: Last person in line shouldn't keep waving — nobody is behind them

Name: Image-To-Text Gutter
What it does (technical): figure + p, img + p { margin-top: 6mm } plus figure { margin-right: 8mm } for inline-floated images
How it helps automated designs: A single gutter constant (~8mm / 32px) covers 90% of image-text adjacencies and eliminates the ''text licking the photo edge'' tell
Drawbacks: Too generous a gutter on small slides creates orphan-y captions; scale gutter to page width
Plain-language explanation: Don't push text against the edge of a photo — give it breathing room, like the white space around a museum placard

Name: Footer Band Padding
What it does (technical): .page { padding-bottom: 1in } .footer { padding-top: 0.5in; border-top: 1px solid var(--sage) } — guaranteed band between body and footer chrome
How it helps automated designs: Body content can stop anywhere; footer band hides variable cut and gives every page the same closing rhythm
Drawbacks: Reduces usable area; conflicts with full-bleed photo pages
Plain-language explanation: Every letter ends with ''Sincerely'' and a signature — the footer band is the signature line on every page

Name: Object-Fit Cover With Focal Position
What it does (technical): img { object-fit: cover; object-position: 50% 30% } — PIL: ImageOps.fit(img, (w,h), centering=(0.5, 0.3)); sharp .resize(...,{fit:'cover',position:'attention'})
How it helps automated designs: Decouples image dimensions from layout cell — the composer asserts the slot, the image complies, no aspect-ratio reasoning at template time
Drawbacks: Default 50% 50% clips heads, watermarks, baked-in captions; requires per-image focal point for portraits
Plain-language explanation: Cropping a photo into a fixed picture frame — instead of resizing the frame, you slide the photo around behind the glass until the important part shows
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Object-Fit Contain For Logos
What it does (technical): object-fit: contain plus a matching neutral background — for logos, charts, diagrams; never crop the asset
How it helps automated designs: Guarantees nothing critical (legend text, axis labels, logomark counter-shape) is clipped — letterboxing is the price of integrity
Drawbacks: Unequal whitespace bars break edge-of-grid alignment; needs same-tone fill
Plain-language explanation: Like packing fragile cargo — the box may have empty corners, but nothing gets cut

Name: Face-Aware Smart Crop
What it does (technical): OpenCV Haar cascade or mediapipe.solutions.face_detection → bbox → compute eye-line → place at the 1/3 horizontal line; saliency fallback when no face is found
How it helps automated designs: Headshots auto-place with eyes on the upper third regardless of source framing — eliminates the ''decapitation'' failure of center-crops
Drawbacks: Haar misses 15-20% of faces; MediaPipe is heavier; group photos need union-rect heuristic
Plain-language explanation: A passport-photo booth that swivels until your eyes hit the marked line — except automated

Name: Lead-Room Nose-Room Placement
What it does (technical): Detect gaze direction; place subject on the third opposite to gaze so 2/3 of the frame is in front of them. Cheap heuristic: face center vs image center
How it helps automated designs: Stops auto-crop from ''trapping'' a subject against the edge they are facing — valuable for editorial pages featuring people
Drawbacks: Requires gaze inference; mirror-flipping breaks photos with visible text
Plain-language explanation: If a person is looking right, leave more space on the right so it feels like they're looking into something instead of being shoved against a wall

Name: Headroom Above Eyebrows
What it does (technical): After face detect: headroom = face_top - crop_top; enforce headroom ≥ 0.10 × face_height. If violated, expand crop upward
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates the iconic ''AI cropping fail'' of eyes at top edge with no forehead — single hard rule, trivial to implement
Drawbacks: Forces sacrifice elsewhere (often chops shoulders/torso) — acceptable trade
Plain-language explanation: A face cut off above the eyebrows looks like a horror-movie poster — always leave forehead air

Name: Aspect-Ratio Enum
What it does (technical): Constrain template slots to a small enum: {16:9, 4:3, 3:2, 1:1, 9:16, 21:9}; at ingest snap each incoming image to the nearest enum and Hungarian-match across the document for variety
How it helps automated designs: Makes the layout solver tractable — only ~6 cell shapes; the same image can be re-used at different ratios from one stored focal point
Drawbacks: Source images at extreme ratios (panoramas, tall food photography) waste pixels
Plain-language explanation: Like clothing sizes — instead of bespoke tailoring per photo, pick the nearest standard cut. Six sizes covers 95%

Name: Smart Crop Saliency Fallback
What it does (technical): cv2.saliency.StaticSaliencyFineGrained_create().computeSaliency(img) returns a heatmap; threshold at >0.6 → bbox → use as focal region
How it helps automated designs: Generalizes smart-crop beyond faces — works on product photography, food, architectural shots, anywhere the subject is not a person
Drawbacks: Saliency is brittle on busy backgrounds — heatmap spreads everywhere; wrap in try/except with center-crop fallback
Plain-language explanation: When there is no face to lock onto, find the brightest, most ''interesting'' patch and crop toward it — a digital eye-tracker

Name: Cover Gradient Scrim
What it does (technical): linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(22,22,22,0.25) 0%, rgba(22,22,22,0.55) 65%, rgba(22,22,22,0.85) 100%) as absolutely-positioned overlay on cover photos
How it helps automated designs: Brand photos vary in tonal value; the 3-stop gradient keeps eyebrow text readable at the top and white title text readable at the bottom regardless of underlying image
Drawbacks: On night photography adds dark vignette to an already-dark area; hardcoded vertical direction
Plain-language explanation: Like a photographer's graduated ND filter — darkens the bottom so the foreground text is always readable
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Photo-Break Side Gradient
What it does (technical): linear-gradient(to right, rgba(70,93,83,0.7) 0%, transparent 60%) — darkens left ~60% of a full-bleed photo where text is overlaid; pair with .photo-break-text { max-width: 500px }
How it helps automated designs: Text in photo-break panels is always readable on the darkened side without the agent knowing anything about the specific photograph
Drawbacks: Right-subject photographs have darkened region falling on the subject; assumes usable negative space on left
Plain-language explanation: Like sunglasses you put on the same side of your face every time — dimming the photo on the left so the white headline always stays readable.
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Caption Band Gradient
What it does (technical): On photo cells: linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(0,0,0,0) 0%, rgba(0,0,0,0.75) 100%) with caption text in 7pt uppercase white, 8mm top padding so gradient fades in before reaching the caption
How it helps automated designs: Photo captions overlay the image with a darkening gradient behind them; gradient prevents text disappearing against light areas
Drawbacks: On small secondary images the 8mm top padding may leave very little visible photo above the gradient
Plain-language explanation: Like a photo credit burned into the corner of a press photograph — the caption lives on the image itself
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Background-Image Desaturation Dim
What it does (technical): filter: saturate(0.4) brightness(0.6) on background images, or composite an rgba(0,0,0,0.45) overlay; PIL: ImageEnhance.Color + Brightness
How it helps automated designs: Auto-placed text over arbitrary photos becomes legible without per-image color selection — composer always uses white text on dimmed image
Drawbacks: Photos lose punch; for brand-hero spreads where the photo is the message, defer to a ''photo-pure'' template with no overlay
Plain-language explanation: Like turning down the music so people can hear you talk — dim the photo so the words land

Name: Image Bleed Outside Grid
What it does (technical): Photo break or full-bleed elements placed at top-level document structure (outside .grid > .row > .col-*) so they truly run edge-to-edge at any viewport
How it helps automated designs: Inside .grid containers max-width and side padding inset photo-break elements; placing them outside lets them bleed edge-to-edge
Drawbacks: Requires the agent to remember a structural exception to the standard nesting pattern
Plain-language explanation: Like a magazine spread that bleeds a photo to the physical edge of the page rather than stopping at the text margin
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Photo Budget Per Spread
What it does (technical): Layout solver constraint: n_images_per_spread ≤4 with exactly_one(image.role == ''hero''); hero gets ≥40% of usable area, supporters ≤20% each
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the ''image dump'' failure where the generator pastes all 12 available photos onto one page — forces editorial restraint
Drawbacks: Long-form content with 30 images needs pagination logic to distribute across spreads
Plain-language explanation: Every spread gets one star and a small chorus — more than that and the eye does not know where to land
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Visual Weight Balance Score
What it does (technical): Compute weight per image as area × (1 - mean_lightness); sum left vs right half of spread. If |left - right| / total > 0.4, flag layout for swap
How it helps automated designs: Symmetrical balance score is a single number the solver can optimize — prevents top-heavy / left-heavy spreads that feel tilted
Drawbacks: Intentional asymmetry (deliberate hero on right) gets flagged; needs override flag
Plain-language explanation: If a heavy dark photo lives on the left, the right side needs something to push back — even if that something is generous whitespace
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Same-Direction Gaze Pairs
What it does (technical): Detect dominant gaze vector per photo (face landmarks + nose-direction); when placing two portraits side-by-side, prefer pairs whose gazes converge inward or both look outward toward a shared third element
How it helps automated designs: Prevents ''two strangers looking opposite directions'' weirdness on team pages or split-portrait spreads
Drawbacks: Mirror-flipping to fix gaze breaks photos with visible text (signage, branding)
Plain-language explanation: Two portraits next to each other should look at each other, or both look outward together — not turn their backs

Name: Pad Don't Crop Logos
What it does (technical): Two-tier role system: role: photo → smart-crop allowed; role: asset → pad-only (ImageOps.pad with matching background). Detect via filename/role tag (logo, headshot, signature)
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates catastrophic failure of arbitrarily lopping off a face or logomark; default to role: asset for any filename containing logo, headshot, portrait, signature
Drawbacks: Requires upstream metadata tagging; misclassification still possible
Plain-language explanation: A logo isn't a photo — you don't crop the corner off the FedEx mark because the slot is square. Pad it

Name: Vignette-To-Edge For Text Overlap
What it does (technical): mask-image: linear-gradient(to right, transparent 0%, black 30%) to fade an image's left edge into a text column; pre-render fallback as PNG
How it helps automated designs: Lets a full-bleed photo absorb a text column without a hard edge or colored panel — useful for covers and section openers
Drawbacks: CSS masks have inconsistent Puppeteer/WeasyPrint support — test on the actual renderer
Plain-language explanation: Instead of a hard photo edge meeting text, soften the photo to a whisper where the words begin

Name: Caption Spatial Contiguity
What it does (technical): Captions, axis labels, legends sit within ~6-10mm of the artifact. No floating corner legend. Captions never wrap over the figure
How it helps automated designs: Auto-gen routinely places captions in a separate template row ''because the grid said so'' — spatial contiguity overrides the template
Drawbacks: Disrupts regular grids; tight layouts can collide caption and figure
Plain-language explanation: A museum puts the placard next to the painting, not around the corner

Name: Avoid Orphan Caption
What it does (technical): figure { break-inside: avoid; page-break-inside: avoid } plus figcaption { break-before: avoid } — and validate caption page-index against image page-index post-render
How it helps automated designs: One CSS line covers 90% of caption-photo splits — browser engines respect break-inside: avoid for figures
Drawbacks: Forces image to next page if it doesn't fit (creates upstream whitespace orphan); pre-size figures ≤0.85× page height
Plain-language explanation: Don't strand a caption alone on the next page — the photo and its label belong together

Name: Avoid Page-Break Inside Chunks
What it does (technical): figure, table, blockquote, .metric-card, .signature-block { break-inside: avoid-page }; h1, h2, h3 { break-after: avoid-page }. Equivalent controls in print engines: \nobreak (TeX), Keep with Next (InDesign) — heading→first-paragraph keep fixes ~80% of stranded-heading cases.
How it helps automated designs: Stops chart caption being orphaned, heading sitting alone at page bottom, signature splitting across leaves — the heading rule alone fixes 80% of auto-gen tells
Drawbacks: Over-applying creates large bottom voids; pair with break-before: page on chapter starts
Plain-language explanation: Tell the page-breaker ''don't slice this thing in half'' and ''don't leave a heading lonely at the bottom''
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Running Header Via String-Set
What it does (technical): h1.chapter { string-set: chap-title content() } then @page :right { @top-right { content: string(chap-title, first-except) } } — first-except suppresses on chapter-start
How it helps automated designs: Once H1 carries the title, every subsequent page header is correct after re-flow — survives content edits
Drawbacks: Not supported in raw Chrome print-to-PDF — needs a paged-media engine (Prince, PagedJS, WeasyPrint)
Plain-language explanation: Like a sticky note that updates itself — the page-top label always shows whichever chapter you're inside
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: TOC With Leader Dots
What it does (technical): nav#toc a::after { content: leader('.') target-counter(attr(href), page) } — Prince/AH/PDFreactor only; flexbox-dot fallback for others
How it helps automated designs: Removes the single most fragile manual editing step in long-form auto-gen — TOC and ''see page N'' computed in the paging engine
Drawbacks: leader() is Prince/AH/PDFreactor only; flexbox-dot fallback floats one px above baseline
Plain-language explanation: The dotted lines in a dinner-party menu connecting ''Salade Niçoise ........... $24'' — auto-drawn

Name: Target-Counter Cross-References
What it does (technical): a.xref::after { content: '' (page '' target-counter(attr(href, url), page) '')'' } — TOC, ''see page 47'' callouts, back-of-book index
How it helps automated designs: All cross-references auto-update on re-pagination; no second pagination pass
Drawbacks: Chrome / wkhtmltopdf / Puppeteer headless do NOT implement — Prince/AntennaHouse/PagedJS only; silent failure
Plain-language explanation: Like the index in the back of a textbook that re-checks every page number right before the book is bound.
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, design-variants, forge + outside research

Name: PDF Bookmarks From Headings
What it does (technical): h1 { bookmark-level: 1; bookmark-label: content(); bookmark-state: open } — PDF outline (Acrobat sidebar) generated directly from semantics
How it helps automated designs: Reviewers jump sections without scrolling; zero extra markup beyond heading levels
Drawbacks: Chromium doesn't emit; Prince/WeasyPrint/AntennaHouse do; for Chromium post-process with pdf-lib/qpdf
Plain-language explanation: Every chapter heading drops a pin in the PDF sidebar

Name: Roman Front-Matter Numbering
What it does (technical): Two named @page rules: @page frontmatter { ... counter(page, lower-roman) } and @page body { ... }; apply via section.front { page: frontmatter } and section.body { page: body; counter-reset: page 1 }
How it helps automated designs: Universal book-grade typography signal: i, ii, iii on front-matter then 1, 2, 3 on the body — institutional-publishing recognition cue with one CSS class flip
Drawbacks: Some engines historically refused to reset built-in page counter; Chromium doesn't honor
Plain-language explanation: The ''i, ii, iii'' pages before ''page 1'' actually starts at Chapter 1 — tiny detail, huge signal

Name: Recto Chapter Starts
What it does (technical): section.chapter { break-before: recto } (modern) or page-break-before: right (legacy) — forces a blank verso so every chapter opens on the right page
How it helps automated designs: One-line stylesheet equals institutional book look
Drawbacks: Adds blank pages so page count balloons; wasted on single-page-scroll PDFs
Plain-language explanation: Always starting a new chapter on the right page of an open book — like a real hardcover

Name: Skip Folio On Chapter Opener
What it does (technical): @page chapter-opener { @bottom-center { content: none } } plus section.chapter > h1 { page: chapter-opener } — first page has no folio but counter still increments
How it helps automated designs: Clean chapter-opener pages without manual deletion
Drawbacks: Requires named-page support (non-Chromium)
Plain-language explanation: When a chapter starts on its own page, you usually don't see ''page 23'' cluttering the bottom

Name: Zero-Padded Two-Digit Numbering
What it does (technical): section_counter and page_no both formatted as f''{n:02d}'' — section numbers and page numbers always two digits, padded with leading zero
How it helps automated designs: Keeps footer text width constant across single- and double-digit values so the right edge of the footer never shifts
Drawbacks: Zero-padding is only correct up to 99 pages/sections
Plain-language explanation: Like a film timecode that always shows 00:01:23 — the leading zero keeps the page count's width constant

Name: Deferred Total-Page Token
What it does (technical): TOTAL_TOKEN = ''__TOTAL__''. Stamp every page footer with the token during build; after all pages accumulate, one string-replace resolves to the zero-padded total
How it helps automated designs: Every page can reference total page count even though the count is unknown during single-page rendering
Drawbacks: Any YAML content containing the literal __TOTAL__ would be corrupted; hardcoded fallbacks (e.g., ''38'') go stale
Plain-language explanation: Like a mail-merge {TOTAL_PAGES} placeholder filled in only once the printer knows how many pages there are
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Continued From On Tokens
What it does (technical): <aside class=''cont-on'' data-target=''#sec-4''></aside> plus aside.cont-on::after { content: ''continues on page '' target-counter(attr(data-target, url), page) }
How it helps automated designs: Honest signal for long tables/lists spanning pages — high recognition in financial documents (loan tape continuations)
Drawbacks: Needs an anchor on the next element so requires two-pass generation or post-render fixup
Plain-language explanation: The ''story continued on page B7'' tag at the bottom of a newspaper article

Name: End-Of-Section Ornament
What it does (technical): section.chapter > *:last-child::after { content: ''✦''; display: block; text-align: center; margin-top: 1em; color: var(--accent) }
How it helps automated designs: Disambiguates ''is this section over or just more of it?'' — especially useful when sections don't force a page break
Drawbacks: Looks twee if every paragraph gets one
Plain-language explanation: The ornament symbol at the end of a magazine article (✦ or ◆) telling you ''story ends here''

Name: Hyperlinked TOC
What it does (technical): Plain Section 3 converted by all major paged-media engines into PDF internal link; in PPTX use run.hyperlink.address
How it helps automated designs: Clickable TOC is a screen-only nav primitive that costs literally nothing
Drawbacks: Some print workflows flatten hyperlinks
Plain-language explanation: Blue underlined words on a webpage — but baked into the PDF

Name: Per-Section Accent Color
What it does (technical): section[data-accent=''navy''] { --accent: #1f2a44 } section[data-accent=''coral''] { --accent: #e07a5f }; every section-scoped rule uses var(--accent); PPTX: different layout master per section
How it helps automated designs: Section recognition kicks in peripherally — readers know which section by color before reading
Drawbacks: Risk of garish output if not constrained to a curated palette; WCAG contrast still required
Plain-language explanation: Color-coded tabs in a binder — red for Financials, blue for Legal

Name: Printed Thumb Tabs
What it does (technical): @page :right { @right-middle { content: string(section-name); writing-mode: vertical-rl; background: var(--accent) } } with full-bleed print
How it helps automated designs: When printed, fanning pages reveals colored tabs on right edge — instant physical section nav
Drawbacks: Requires bleed-aware setup; on-screen muted
Plain-language explanation: Colored tab strips on the side of a dictionary or Bible

Name: Asymmetric Verso-Recto Headers
What it does (technical): @page :verso { @top-left { content: string(book-title) } } @page :recto { @top-right { content: string(chap-title) } } — book title left, chapter title right
How it helps automated designs: Reader sees both global container and local context at any open spread
Drawbacks: Only meaningful on facing-page layouts
Plain-language explanation: Left page says the book name, right page says the current chapter — you know where you are at two zoom levels

Name: Chapter-Relative Pagination
What it does (technical): @page chapter-N { @bottom-right { content: counter(chapter) ''-'' counter(chap-page) } } with counter-reset: chap-page on every .chapter
How it helps automated designs: Long technical manuals (loan docket binders, legal exhibits) read more cleanly as ''Exhibit C, page 4'' than ''page 312''
Drawbacks: Non-standard in trade books
Plain-language explanation: A tabbed manual reads ''Section 3, page 7'' instead of ''page 312'' — easier to find with thumb tabs

Name: Narrative Arc Sequencing
What it does (technical): Page order: Thesis → Evidence → Team → Structure → Risk → Action; QA Narrative Position dimension deducts when a Risk page appears before Thesis
How it helps automated designs: Enforces that page order is not arbitrary — a Risk page appearing before Thesis scores poorly
Drawbacks: Prescriptive for fundraising documents — creative or non-standard structures generate false negatives
Plain-language explanation: Pages must appear in logical investment-story order — why (thesis), proof (evidence), who (team), how (structure), what could go wrong, now what

Name: Multi-Column Body With Span Heads
What it does (technical): .body { column-count: 2; column-gap: 6mm } plus h2 { column-span: all; break-after: column } — text snakes across columns, headings span both
How it helps automated designs: Halves page count vs single-column for text-heavy memos; section heads still span both columns
Drawbacks: column-span: all is patchy in older Prince; figures inside columns may overflow
Plain-language explanation: Newspaper columns — text snakes down one column, jumps to the next, but headlines stretch across both
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: At-Page Size And Zero Margin
What it does (technical): @page { size: letter; margin: 0 } plus .page { width: 8.5in; height: 11in; padding: 0.75in 0.75in 1in; box-sizing: border-box }
How it helps automated designs: Bypasses Chromium's default 0.4-1.25in margins that silently clip content or insert blank trailing pages — verified live OKOA Ascent rebuild
Drawbacks: Lose Chromium's built-in URL/date footer
Plain-language explanation: Strip the printer's picture frame and design your own inside the canvas

Name: Last-Page Break Suppression
What it does (technical): .page:last-of-type { page-break-after: auto } — overrides the universal .page { page-break-after: always }
How it helps automated designs: Puppeteer otherwise emits a blank trailing page after the closing panel — every doc auto-ends with a closing page so one rule eliminates the blank-page defect universally
Drawbacks: Multi-doc batches break last-of-type; any invisible div injected after the closing breaks it silently
Plain-language explanation: Tell the printer ''stop after the last sheet'' — without it every job ejects a blank trailing sheet

Name: Puppeteer Bottom-Margin Defense
What it does (technical): Use @page { size: letter; margin: 0 } OR .page { height: 9.75in } upfront — never rely on the default 1.25in bottom margin that creates blank trailing pages when paired with .page { height: 11in }
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates blank trailing pages caused by Puppeteer's hardcoded bottom-margin assumption
Drawbacks: Loses the Chromium default footer line; must implement your own footer chrome
Plain-language explanation: Like a printer that secretly keeps an inch at the bottom for itself — either tell it 'no inch for you' or shrink your page to fit what it leaves you.
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Strip Lazy-Loading Before Render
What it does (technical): Before Puppeteer/Playwright PDF export: html = html.replace(/loading=[''\"]lazy[''\"]/g, '''') — IntersectionObserver never fires for offscreen images in headless mode
How it helps automated designs: Without it, multi-page documents render with broken images below the fold — verified in-repo failure (Ascent BRAD rebuild 2026-05-22)
Drawbacks: Eager-loads all images so RAM during render is higher; for 100+ image documents batch render or raise V8 heap
Plain-language explanation: Lazy-loading photos pretend to wait until you scroll near them — in a printer that doesn't scroll, they never load at all
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Wait For Fonts.Ready Before Capture
What it does (technical): @font-face { font-display: block } plus await page.evaluateHandle('document.fonts.ready') before page.pdf()
How it helps automated designs: If page.pdf() fires before fonts.ready, the PDF embeds Times fallback and typographic identity silently collapses
Drawbacks: networkidle0 can stall on analytics beacons
Plain-language explanation: Wait for the typeface to actually show up before taking the photograph
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Font Subsetting And Embedding
What it does (technical): @font-face with woff2 base64 inline plus pyftsubset font.woff2 --text-file=document.txt --layout-features=''*'' to keep OpenType features
How it helps automated designs: Embedded fonts guarantee identical render on every device; subsetting drops 600KB serif to 80KB
