Drawbacks: Subsetting can break OpenType features if glyph tables drop — preserve with --layout-features=''*''
Plain-language explanation: Glue the typefaces into the PDF so they travel with it — the reader can't substitute Times by accident

Name: ICC Color Tagging
What it does (technical): For Prince: @prince-pdf { prince-pdf-output-intent: url(''sRGB_v4_ICC_preference.icc'') }; for Chromium post-process via Ghostscript color conversion
How it helps automated designs: Untagged PDFs render with viewer-default color spaces so ''warm white #FBF8F2'' looks subtly different in Acrobat vs Preview vs iPad
Drawbacks: Offset wants CMYK; PDF/X-1a requires CMYK plus no transparency
Plain-language explanation: Stamp the PDF with its color recipe so every viewer cooks it the same way

Name: Print-Color-Adjust Exact
What it does (technical): @media print { * { print-color-adjust: exact; -webkit-print-color-adjust: exact } }
How it helps automated designs: Browsers default to stripping backgrounds at print to save ink; for brand-styled PDFs this is non-negotiable
Drawbacks: User print dialog can override (only relevant for live print, irrelevant for page.pdf())
Plain-language explanation: Tell the printer: no ink-saving creativity, print every pixel as designed

Name: Full-Bleed Bleed And Marks
What it does (technical): @page { bleed: 0.125in; marks: crop cross; margin: 0 } plus .page::before with background image extended -0.125in
How it helps automated designs: Guarantees ink-to-edge for full-bleed images — survives guillotine drift (~1/16in)
Drawbacks: Chromium ignores bleed/marks; WeasyPrint buggy; Prince handles correctly
Plain-language explanation: Print slightly bigger than the page so the cutter never reveals white slivers
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Box-Decoration-Break Clone
What it does (technical): .callout { box-decoration-break: clone; -webkit-box-decoration-break: clone }
How it helps automated designs: Default slice shears off background/border at page break; clone re-paints decoration on every fragment
Drawbacks: Chrome ≤129 supported inline only; Chrome 130+ (Oct 2024) ships full block-level + unprefixed support. Safari still inline-only. WeasyPrint/Prince block-level. Keep -webkit- prefix for legacy Chromium.
Plain-language explanation: If you cut the card in half, re-frame both halves so each has a complete border

Name: Section Rotation For Landscape Inserts
What it does (technical): @page landscape { size: 11in 8.5in } plus .financial-table { page: landscape; break-before: page; break-after: page }
How it helps automated designs: Wide tables (cap stacks, financial models) read terribly in portrait; named @page lets specific sections rotate
Drawbacks: Chromium ignores named pages entirely — must split into two PDFs and merge
Plain-language explanation: Wide spreadsheet gets turned sideways like a fold-out map in a guidebook

Name: At-Page First Cover Chrome
What it does (technical): @page :first { @top-right { content: none } } @page :left { margin-left: 1.25in } — cover stays clean, interior pages get running heads, gutters mirror
How it helps automated designs: Cover stays clean; interior pages get running heads; gutters mirror automatically
Drawbacks: Chromium accepts selectors but doesn't render @top-* / @bottom-* margin boxes — WeasyPrint/Prince/PagedJS do
Plain-language explanation: Like a wedding invitation where the front stays clean and the inside pages have a discreet header — the cover is formal, the interior helps you navigate.

Name: Watermark Via At-Page Background
What it does (technical): @page { background-image: url(''data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg>...DRAFT...</svg>''); background-position: center }
How it helps automated designs: Document-wide watermark in one place — no per-page injection
Drawbacks: Chromium doesn't paint @page backgrounds; WeasyPrint/Prince/PagedJS do
Plain-language explanation: ''DRAFT'' stamp lives in the page template, not on every sheet manually

Name: Image-Rendering Hint And 2x Authoring
What it does (technical): img.logo { image-rendering: -webkit-optimize-contrast; image-rendering: crisp-edges } plus author images at 2× final print size
How it helps automated designs: Most ''looks AI-generated'' PDFs are actually ''looks 96-DPI'' PDFs; 2× authoring with explicit hints produces 300-DPI output
Drawbacks: crisp-edges ruins photographs — surgical use on logos/icons only
Plain-language explanation: Hand the printer photos at twice the size they'll appear, and tell them which are photographs (smooth) and which are logos (sharp)

Name: DPI Tier Discipline
What it does (technical): Downsample every image to the maximum DPI required by its largest deployed slot: target_px = slot_inches × target_dpi. Use PIL Image.LANCZOS for downsampling, never upsample silently
How it helps automated designs: A 12-MP source in a 2in×2in 300-DPI slot is 4× oversized; pre-downsampling saves 10-50× PDF size
Drawbacks: Irreversible — always keep originals and downsample the delivery copy
Plain-language explanation: Use just enough resolution for the destination — web=72, OK-print=150, sharp-print=300, gallery=600

Name: 16:9 Default Aspect Ratio
What it does (technical): prs.slide_width = Emu(12192000); prs.slide_height = Emu(6858000) — type screen16x9; reserve screen4x3 only for legacy projectors
How it helps automated designs: Single canonical canvas means one layout math, no branching for legacy 4:3
Drawbacks: Legacy projectors and some handouts still want 4:3; vertical/social needs 9:16 master
Plain-language explanation: Like choosing widescreen versus old-TV — pick widescreen unless you know the screen is square

Name: Slide Safe-Area Inset
What it does (technical): Reserve ~0.5in (457200 EMU) on all four edges on a 16:9 letterbox; encode via slide-layout placeholder <a:xfrm> rather than per-shape so every slide inherits
How it helps automated designs: Prevents body content from kissing the bezel on projector overscan; guarantees print-bleed cutoff doesn't lose text
Drawbacks: Full-bleed photo slides intentionally violate the safe area — needs a layout flag
Plain-language explanation: Like writing inside the painted lines of a parking spot — even if the car fits on the line, it looks polished when it doesn't

Name: Sentence-Title Takeaway
What it does (technical): Title placeholder = a complete sentence stating the takeaway, not a topic label. Cap at ~90 chars to fit one line at 28-32pt. LLM prompt: title = the conclusion, not the topic
How it helps automated designs: LLMs already write summary sentences — emit one as the title and the body is freed to support it; QA can grade ''does body support headline?''
Drawbacks: Some corporate templates expect noun-phrase titles (''Q3 Performance''); style guide may forbid
Plain-language explanation: The slide title is the punchline, not the topic of the joke

Name: One Message Per Slide
What it does (technical): A slide may contain ≤1 H1 + ≤1 body block + ≤1 visual; Gamma's card system makes this default. Auto-split overflow content into a sibling slide rather than shrinking type
How it helps automated designs: Auto-splitting is mechanical (regex split on H1); shrinking type is quality-debt landmine
Drawbacks: Inflates slide count — conflicts with Kawasaki's 10-slide ceiling; use when audience reads, not watches
Plain-language explanation: Each slide gets exactly one thing to say, like an index card on a corkboard

Name: 6x6 Bullet Cap
What it does (technical): Validator: len(bullets) ≤ 6 AND max(words_per_bullet) ≤ 6. If violated, split slide, collapse to one sentence, or demote to slidedoc layout
How it helps automated designs: Hard numeric cap is the easiest validator to write; output stays parseable in a 5-second glance
Drawbacks: Treats all content as outline-shaped; loses nuance Tufte criticizes
Plain-language explanation: No more than six bullets, no more than six words each — like a tweet broken into a list

Name: 30pt Minimum Body Font Kawasaki
What it does (technical): paragraph.font.size = Pt(30) as floor on body placeholders; titles 36-44pt; disable PowerPoint auto-fit shrink
How it helps automated designs: Forces upstream content compression; auto-overflow becomes a deterministic ''split slide'' branch
Drawbacks: Slidedocs (read, not presented) intentionally use 11-14pt; rule must be mode-gated
Plain-language explanation: If you can't read it from the back row, the slide is wrong — not the room

Name: Disable Native Auto-Fit
What it does (technical): tf.auto_size = MSO_AUTO_SIZE.NONE in python-pptx OR <a:bodyPr><a:noAutofit/></a:bodyPr> in OOXML
How it helps automated designs: Outputs reproducible across PowerPoint / Keynote / LibreOffice renderers — no surprise 11-pt slides where Office silently shrank the text
Drawbacks: Costs the free ''shrink to fit'' fallback; you must implement split-on-overflow
Plain-language explanation: Lock the text box so PowerPoint can't secretly shrink your font behind your back

Name: Slide Layout Typology
What it does (technical): Author 5-7 slide layouts: title, section-divider, content-1col, content-2col, full-bleed-image, data-chart, quote, closer. Each layout pre-positions title, body, footer, and picture placeholder
How it helps automated designs: LLM classifies each input chunk → picks a layout enum → one branch per layout. Mechanical and testable
Drawbacks: Adding a new content shape later means editing master XML, not just slides
Plain-language explanation: Like pre-printed forms for different types of content — fill in the blanks instead of designing each page from scratch

Name: Bottom-Pinned Slide Footer
What it does (technical): Three placeholders on the master at y = slide_height - 360000 EMU (~0.4in from bottom): left = logo (picture placeholder), center = section, right = <a:fld type=''slidenum''/>. Anchor MSO_ANCHOR.BOTTOM
How it helps automated designs: Generator writes nothing to the master — placeholders self-populate from layout inheritance + slide-number field auto-counts
Drawbacks: Section field needs a custom XML property plus section-number tracking
Plain-language explanation: Every slide gets a small badge at the bottom — logo on the left, what section you're in, what page you're on
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Master-Defined Vertical Rhythm
What it does (technical): Master-level <a:bodyPr lIns=''91440'' tIns=''45720'' rIns=''91440'' bIns=''45720''> plus <a:spcBef><a:spcPts val=''600''/></a:spcBef> (6pt before each paragraph)
How it helps automated designs: A single value change in the master cascades to every slide; generator emits no inline spacing
Drawbacks: Inheritance is silent — if a slide overrides locally, debugging requires XML diff
Plain-language explanation: Set the line-spacing once in the template and every slide inherits — like CSS variables for slides
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Section Divider Slides
What it does (technical): Dedicated section-divider layout with saturated background fill, large numeral (''02''), and section title. Generator inserts before any chapter transition. Color cycles through 3-6 swatches
How it helps automated designs: Visual pause — reader's eye resets — without writing transition animations
Drawbacks: Adds slide count; conflicts with 10-slide pitches
Plain-language explanation: A bold full-color slide that says ''Section 2: Market'' — like a chapter title page in a book

Name: Full-Bleed Image With Scrim
What it does (technical): Picture shape sized to full slide plus MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE overlay at 40-60% black, or <a:gradFill> from transparent to 70% black covering the lower third. Title placeholder lifted above scrim with white text
How it helps automated designs: Image carries the message; scrim is a single rectangle the generator always adds — no per-image contrast checking needed at minimum 50% opacity
Drawbacks: Some images become illegible regardless; ideally measure luminance under title region before falling back
Plain-language explanation: Big photo, dark gradient on the bottom so the white words still read
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Chart Slide One Chart One Sentence
What it does (technical): python-pptx chart.has_gridlines = False; one chart shape per slide; title placeholder = the takeaway (''Revenue grew 38% YoY''); axis labels at 18pt; data labels on highest 1-2 points only
How it helps automated designs: Tufte-style high data-ink ratio falls out of removing default chrome — every default-off is one fewer parameter
Drawbacks: Removing gridlines from non-time-series scatterplots can hurt comparison; gate on chart type
Plain-language explanation: One chart, one sentence saying what it proves, no extra lines or labels cluttering it

Name: Quote Slide Layout
What it does (technical): Body placeholder at ~44pt italic centered, attribution placeholder at 18pt regular below right-aligned with em-dash prefix; smart-quotes mandatory
How it helps automated designs: Whenever input matches quote: ''...'', by: ''...'' schema, this layout fires deterministically
Drawbacks: Over-use makes a deck feel like a Pinterest board
Plain-language explanation: Big curly quote in italic, name underneath — the ''framed quote on the wall'' slide

Name: Build Reveal Sequencing
What it does (technical): OOXML <p:timing> with <p:par> containing <p:cTn> nodes per paragraph; presetID=''1'' (appear) per bullet; write XML directly into slide.element via lxml
How it helps automated designs: Reveals control pace without splitting into N slides; preserves the 10-slide budget
Drawbacks: Animations look amateur if overused (Reynolds: ''weapons of distraction''); printed handouts collapse builds
Plain-language explanation: Bullets appear one at a time on click — like flashcards inside one slide

Name: Z-Pattern Coordinate Anchors
What it does (technical): OOXML title x=457200, y=457200; visual x=7200000, y=457200; CTA x=9000000, y=6000000 — hard-coded positions for content-with-CTA slide-type
How it helps automated designs: Hard-coded grid coordinates per layout — no aesthetic decision at runtime
Drawbacks: RTL languages reverse the pattern; need locale-aware layout flipping
Plain-language explanation: Eyes start top-left and zig-zag to bottom-right — put the important stuff on that path

Name: Image Position Heuristic
What it does (technical): Layout templates enforce picture placeholder positions in {top-band, right-column, full-bleed}. Never auto-emit a layout where picture occupies bottom-left while text occupies top-right (anti-Z)
How it helps automated designs: Mechanical CI assertion catches accidentally-bad layouts at generation time
Drawbacks: Some intentional contra-Z layouts (e.g., a ''footer'' author portrait) are valid exceptions and need opt-out
Plain-language explanation: Pictures go up top or on the right — not tucked into the lower-left corner
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Slidedoc Dense Reading Mode
What it does (technical): Separate master with 14pt body, 1.25 line-spacing, 2-column body placeholders, no title placeholder on every slide; generator switches when --mode=slidedoc
How it helps automated designs: Single mode flag flips the entire style sheet; same content tree renders differently for read-vs-present
Drawbacks: Two parallel masters to maintain; output is a document, not a presentation — don't project it
Plain-language explanation: Sometimes the deck is a handout to read alone, not a slideshow — use a denser layout for that

Name: Smart-Layout Fallback Chain
What it does (technical): For each slide rank N candidate layouts by content fit (number of bullets, image presence, table shape); emit #1, expose #2-#5 as ''swap layout'' options via sidecar JSON
How it helps automated designs: Editor sees options, not a blank choice — feels less ''AI-rigid''
Drawbacks: Memory cost; only 2-3 alternates usually viewed
Plain-language explanation: The system picks one layout but keeps two spares ready in case you want to swap

Name: Maximize Data-Ink Ratio
What it does (technical): matplotlib ax.spines['top'/'right'].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(length=0); plotly fig.update_layout(plot_bgcolor='white', xaxis_showgrid=False); chart.js scales.x.grid.display=false
How it helps automated designs: One-line config delta lifts default chart from ''Excel screenshot'' to ''publication-grade''
Drawbacks: Tufte's minimalism is empirically less memorable than mildly-decorated charts (Bateman 2010)
Plain-language explanation: Wiping fingerprints off a glass display case — you actually see what's inside

Name: No 3D Charts
What it does (technical): Hard ban: refuse chart_type in {bar3d, pie3d, surface3d}
How it helps automated designs: Single boolean filter at chart-router level; eliminates perception-distortion class without judgement
Drawbacks: Genuine 3D data (terrain, volumetric) loses renderer
Plain-language explanation: Reading a price tag through a beveled magnifying glass — the price changes depending on the angle

Name: Cap Pies At 5 Slices
What it does (technical): if categories > 5: chart_type = ''bar''. Aggregate smallest into ''Other'' if pie unavoidable
How it helps automated designs: Trivial categorical-count check at chart-router
Drawbacks: Loses long-tail visibility
Plain-language explanation: Pies ask your eye to compare angles (we're bad at it). Bars ask you to compare lengths (we evolved to do it)

Name: Donut With Center Stat
What it does (technical): plotly go.Pie(hole=0.55) plus annotation; chart.js doughnut plus center plugin
How it helps automated designs: Center-stat carries headline; slices give breakdown — the only acceptable pie variant
Drawbacks: Center-stat overlaps external labels — disable when on
Plain-language explanation: A donut with a number in the hole is like a pizza with the bill printed in the middle

Name: Y-Axis Starts At Zero
What it does (technical): matplotlib ax.set_ylim(0, ...); plotly yaxis_rangemode='tozero'; chart.js scales.y.beginAtZero: true (bar charts only)
How it helps automated designs: Pure config; eliminates ''deceptive bar chart'' reviewer findings
Drawbacks: Bars in tight ranges look identical — switch chart type, don't break the rule
Plain-language explanation: Bars work because length equals number — cropping the bottom is the real-estate-photo trick that hides the dumpster

Name: Single-Accent Chart Color
What it does (technical): palette = [neutral_gray] × n with palette[highlight] = brand_accent — desaturate every series except the one being argued for
How it helps automated designs: Forces generator to declare what the chart is about
Drawbacks: Requires upstream ''which series matters'' metadata
Plain-language explanation: Turn down every voice in the choir except the one singing the melody
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Viridis For Sequential Colormaps
What it does (technical): matplotlib cmap='viridis'; plotly colorscale='Viridis'; D3 d3.interpolateViridis — CVD-safe and print-safe by construction (monotonic luminance)
How it helps automated designs: Default colormap that works for ~8% of men with colorblindness and survives black-and-white print
Drawbacks: Yellow end of viridis vanishes on light backgrounds
Plain-language explanation: ''Darker = lower, brighter = higher'' works for everyone, including the colorblind. Old rainbow/jet lies — it shows fake stripes

Name: ColorBrewer Family By Data Shape
What it does (technical): Three families: sequential (one-direction magnitude), diverging (signed deviation), qualitative (unordered categories); pick family by inspecting data
How it helps automated designs: Generator picks family by inspecting data — monotone → sequential, signed → diverging, categorical → qualitative
Drawbacks: Wrong family lies about the data
Plain-language explanation: Like picking the right type of map for the data — a thermometer for one-way magnitudes, a thermostat for things measured from a midpoint, sports jerseys for unordered categories.

Name: Categorical Palette Cap At 8
What it does (technical): Cap qualitative palette at 8 distinct hues; beyond, switch to color+pattern encoding
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the ''rainbow legend'' where users can't map swatch to category
Drawbacks: Patterns add visual noise; not all renderers support fills cleanly
Plain-language explanation: A choir has sections — sopranos, altos, tenors, basses; 30 sections is just noise

Name: Horizontal Gridlines Only Light
What it does (technical): ax.yaxis.grid(True, color='#E5E5E5', linewidth=0.5); ax.xaxis.grid(False)
How it helps automated designs: Single style rule removes the ''graph paper'' look
Drawbacks: Sparse gridlines hurt precise reading
Plain-language explanation: Gridlines are like ruled notebook lines — helpful, but if as dark as the handwriting they win the fight. Whisper them
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Direct Labeling Over Legend
What it does (technical): matplotlib ax.text(x[-1], y[-1], label, va='center'); plotly mode='lines+text', textposition='middle right' — label endpoints directly
How it helps automated designs: Endpoints known deterministically; eliminates legend eye-saccades
Drawbacks: Crowded endpoints need de-overlap logic
Plain-language explanation: Instead of ''red line is Apple,'' write ''Apple'' right at the tip — name tags, not a seating chart

Name: Reference Lines Muted
What it does (technical): ax.axhline(target, color='#888', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.75, zorder=0) — drop a line for any target/quota carried by data
How it helps automated designs: If data carries a target, drop the reference line automatically; cap at two
Drawbacks: Cap at two — more crowd the chart quickly
Plain-language explanation: A reference line is the speed limit sign on a chart — instantly shows which bars are speeding
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: 5-7 Round-Number Tick Marks
What it does (technical): matplotlib MaxNLocator(nbins=6, steps=[1,2,2.5,5,10]); plotly nticks=6 — round-number ticks
How it helps automated designs: One-line idiom across libraries
Drawbacks: Fixed step counts can lop off topmost data point
Plain-language explanation: A ruler with marks every 2.7 inches is useless — 0/25/50/75/100 is a ruler people can read
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Horizontal Bars For Long Labels
What it does (technical): First try shorter labels; if still wide, switch to horizontal bar; only rotate as third choice and ≤45°
How it helps automated designs: Decision tree is mechanical and avoids the unreadable-rotated-x-axis failure
Drawbacks: Horizontal bars feel less ''default'' to some audiences
Plain-language explanation: Either shorten the words or rotate the chart — never rotate the reader
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Small Multiples Over Spaghetti
What it does (technical): matplotlib plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, sharey=True); plotly make_subplots with shared range — trigger when n_series > 4
How it helps automated designs: Replaces multi-series ''spaghetti'' with grid of small charts
Drawbacks: Eats real estate; for slides cap at 2×3
Plain-language explanation: Eight lines on one chart is eight conversations at one dinner — eight small charts is eight phone calls, each clear

Name: Sparklines Inline
What it does (technical): D3 inline <svg width=80 height=20> with no axes; pair with current value beside it
How it helps automated designs: Per-row trend at fixed pixel size embedded next to the metric — high data density without a chart slide
Drawbacks: Loses absolute scale — always pair with numeric value
Plain-language explanation: EKG strip next to the patient name — you see the heart racing without needing the full printout

Name: Show Distribution Not Just Mean
What it does (technical): Box plot or violin; strip+jitter for ≤50 points; rule: if coefficient_of_variation > 0.3, refuse a single-mean bar
How it helps automated designs: Variance-based switch prevents misleading single-point summaries
Drawbacks: Executives find box plots foreign — label first use
Plain-language explanation: ''Average commute 30 min'' hides that half take 15 and a quarter take 75 — show the spread

Name: Chart Source And As-Of Date
What it does (technical): Every chart carries ''Source: ...'' and ''As of [date]''; missing either deducts on multiple QA dimensions simultaneously
How it helps automated designs: Forces the data pipeline to carry source metadata and date through to render; documents pass institutional credibility
Drawbacks: Some data legitimately has no ''as of'' (team bios, diagrams) — requires judgement
Plain-language explanation: Every number and chart needs a ''Source:'' line and a date — no source, no pass

Name: Zero-Baseline Axis Honesty
What it does (technical): S5 rubric criterion: axes start at zero or justify truncation with a break marker; truncated axis without justification deducts
How it helps automated designs: Prevents auto-generated charts from using library defaults that start axes at data-min and visually exaggerate differences
Drawbacks: Some chart types (yield comparisons in narrow band) legitimately benefit from truncation
Plain-language explanation: Chart axes must start at zero unless the chart explicitly explains why they don't — a truncated axis that hides zero is a trust violation

Name: Gross Vs Net Comparability
What it does (technical): S5 criterion: comparisons compare comparable things (gross vs gross, not gross vs net); requires data YAML metadata to carry the distinction
How it helps automated designs: Prevents a common PE marketing error that draws regulatory scrutiny
Drawbacks: Reviewer must know which data fields are gross vs net
Plain-language explanation: If you show your fund's gross returns next to a net benchmark, that is a defect — compare like with like

Name: Denominator Clarity
What it does (technical): S5: percentages state what they are a percentage of; chart and metric templates render denominator context alongside
How it helps automated designs: Forces template to render denominator context — '87% LTV' must state 87% of what
Drawbacks: Adds text to already-dense data pages; template designer must decide where denominator lives
Plain-language explanation: ''87%'' means nothing without saying 87% of what — every percentage must state its denominator somewhere on the page

Name: Survivorship Bias Disclosure
What it does (technical): S4 criterion: track record exclusions disclosed; data pipeline carries an exclusions flag and template renders a disclosure when track record is a subset
How it helps automated designs: Required for institutional credibility on private-fund performance pages
Drawbacks: Requires data source to distinguish included vs excluded deals; CLEAN by default if all included
Plain-language explanation: If the performance track record only shows winning deals and quietly excludes losses, that must be stated — silence is a defect

Name: Forward-Looking Triple-Flag
What it does (technical): S3, S4 and S6 dimensions independently penalize projections without caveats — a projection without ''forward-looking'' label loses on three axes
How it helps automated designs: Stacks rubric weight against any projection not flagged — makes 100/100 unachievable without explicit caveats
Drawbacks: Three-dimension redundancy can feel disproportionate for a single missing line
Plain-language explanation: Any projected number must be labeled as a projection with its assumptions or three separate rubric checks will catch it

Name: Past-Performance Disclaimer
What it does (technical): S6 (Compliance): performance pages carry past-performance disclaimer; missing on a performance page is a major defect under a heavier-weighted dimension (+2 severity)
How it helps automated designs: Performance and track-record templates must include boilerplate; failure scores a major deduction on an amplified dimension
Drawbacks: QA only checks presence, not wording accuracy — disclaimer text must be kept legally current
Plain-language explanation: Any page showing returns or track record must carry the past-performance disclaimer — its absence is a major fail

Name: Reg D 506(b) Compliance Check
What it does (technical): S6: no general solicitation; auto-generated cover/subscription pages cannot use language patterns that constitute public solicitation under SEC rules
How it helps automated designs: Prevents major legal defect in private-placement documents
Drawbacks: Reviewer must know current SEC interpretation of ''general solicitation'' — the rubric does not define the boundary
Plain-language explanation: If the document is a private placement under Reg D 506(b), it cannot contain language that looks like a public advertisement

Name: Past Performance Date Anchoring
What it does (technical): S3 and S5: every data point has an ''as of'' date; both dimensions deduct for missing dates
How it helps automated designs: Requires data YAML and templates to carry and display a date field; missing dates fail two rubric dimensions
Drawbacks: Some data has no meaningful ''as of'' date — requires judgement
Plain-language explanation: Every number shown to an LP needs a date — ''Our portfolio is X'' without ''as of Q1 2026'' is a defect

Name: Institutional Peer Benchmark
What it does (technical): E4 (Professional Polish): peer comparison vs top-tier PE fund marketing (BCRED, Apollo, Ares prospectuses); reviewer asks ''would this hold up next to a Blackstone product?''
How it helps automated designs: Sets the quality ceiling at named institutional comparables rather than an abstract ''professional'' bar
Drawbacks: Subjective — requires reviewer familiarity with those materials
Plain-language explanation: The bar for ''professional polish'' is a Blackstone or Apollo fund document — if it would look out of place next to those, it fails

Name: PNG Dimension Cap 2000px
What it does (technical): Verify every PNG is ≤2000px on both edges before any reviewer call; recommended render: pdftoppm -r 150 -png (~1275×1650px for US Letter) or sips -Z 1800 as safety net
How it helps automated designs: Exceeding the Anthropic API cap locks the conversation unrecoverably until /clear — a hard precondition before any review
Drawbacks: Lower DPI reduces fidelity for fine-grained text checks; 150 DPI may miss small-font defects
Plain-language explanation: Every screenshot fed to the reviewer must be no wider and no taller than 2000 pixels, or the conversation goes unresponsive

Name: Compact Cadence Every 8 Pages
What it does (technical): After every ~8 page iterations run /compact to flush old screenshots; the first ''image could not be processed and was removed'' warning means buffer is degraded — stop and compact
How it helps automated designs: Prevents accumulated PNG context from degrading reviewer accuracy on long documents
Drawbacks: /compact discards context — orchestrator must re-establish page-map state after each flush
Plain-language explanation: Like a darkroom that has to dump used developer fluid every few prints — once the chemistry goes off, every photo afterward comes out wrong.
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Wigum Anti-Loop Escalation
What it does (technical): Track per-(criterion_id, page) WARNING occurrences; after 3 consecutive iterations with same WARNING, escalate to ERROR. Reset to 0 for keys not seen in current iteration
How it helps automated designs: Some visual defects are LLM-judgment-dependent — reviewer flips pass/fail on borderline; escalation forces convergence by iteration 3
Drawbacks: Hardcoded 3-iteration threshold; legitimate WARNINGs needing user-side changes artificially escalate
Plain-language explanation: Like a building inspector who gives two warnings before writing a violation — third time is a citation that stops the project

Name: Convergence Gate STALL
What it does (technical): After each Wigum iteration compare deduction count to previous; if same or increased → STALL → escalate to user; loop must show strictly decreasing deductions
How it helps automated designs: Prevents infinite fix-break cycles where fixing one thing breaks another; forces human intervention when the loop is not making progress
Drawbacks: A single introduced defect terminates a loop that was otherwise converging — overly sensitive in early iterations
Plain-language explanation: Every iteration must make things better, not just different — if the score plateaus or drops, stop and ask the human

Name: Per-Page Iteration Ceiling
What it does (technical): Default max 5 iterations per page (configurable); when max is reached → MAX_ITER escalation to user, same flow as STALL
How it helps automated designs: Caps token spend and prevents runaway loops on intractable pages; forces human judgement when automation can't fully resolve a page
Drawbacks: Complex pages may legitimately need more than 5 iterations; default may be too low for dense data pages
Plain-language explanation: The automated fix loop will try at most five times on each page — after five tries, it stops and asks the human what to do

Name: Screenshot Authority Override
What it does (technical): Reviewer only sees the rendered PNG, never source code: ''if it looks wrong in the PNG, it IS wrong — regardless of what the source code says''
How it helps automated designs: Forces QA to catch rendering bugs that exist only at paint time — misaligned elements, wrong font rendering, invisible overlays
Drawbacks: Cannot catch data errors that render correctly (a wrong number displayed cleanly); requires a reliable screenshot pipeline
Plain-language explanation: The screenshot is the final arbiter — a pixel that looks broken is broken, full stop
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa + outside research

Name: Fix-List Independence Wall
What it does (technical): Reviewer prompt explicitly excludes build script path, prior fix list, Fixer notes, and any ''verify that X was fixed'' language
How it helps automated designs: Prevents confirmation bias — the Reviewer cannot be primed to confirm what it expects; each iteration is a genuinely independent evaluation
Drawbacks: Slightly higher token cost; cannot leverage iteration history to speed scoring
Plain-language explanation: Each new reviewer is a fresh pair of eyes with no idea what the previous review said or what was changed

Name: Evidence-Anchored Deductions
What it does (technical): Reviewer quotes specific visual evidence for every deduction: location, text content, background color; ''unreadable at this resolution'' beats guessing
How it helps automated designs: Forces the reviewer to ground every finding in what is actually visible; prevents false positives from hallucinated content
Drawbacks: Adds verbosity to reviewer output; reviewer may still confabulate plausible-sounding visual descriptions
Plain-language explanation: Every defect must be pinned to something the reviewer can actually see — location, words, colors. Guessing is prohibited

Name: Page-Type Severity Weighting
What it does (technical): Heavier dimensions (page-type-specific) apply +2 to deduction severity; lighter dimensions apply -1; 12 page types mapped to heavier/lighter dimensions
How it helps automated designs: A missing source citation on a Market Thesis page scores harder than on a Team page — calibrates QA pressure to what matters per context
Drawbacks: Increases rubric complexity; misclassified page type produces miscalibrated scores
Plain-language explanation: The same flaw counts more on some page types than others — missing source citation hurts a data page more than a team-bio page

Name: Card Baseline Alignment QA
What it does (technical): E2 criterion: card/box alignment — same-level elements share baselines; misaligned cards or boxes on the same visual row are a deductible defect
How it helps automated designs: Catches flexbox and grid layouts where card heights differ and content vertically shifts — common auto-gen failure mode
Drawbacks: No tolerance specified; 1px baseline drift may be indistinguishable from intent in a screenshot
Plain-language explanation: If you have a row of metric cards, their text baselines must line up — cards that don't visually align are a layout defect

Name: Eyebrow Footer Consistency
What it does (technical): E3 cross-page sweep: footer/header consistency — same position, same format across all pages; eyebrow and footer present on every page
How it helps automated designs: Enforces every page carries the brand's navigation strip; catches pages where the template was applied inconsistently
Drawbacks: No specification of what eyebrow must contain — reviewer infers from existing pages
Plain-language explanation: Every page must have its eyebrow and footer, in the same spot, formatted the same way as all the others
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Zero Stray Artifacts
What it does (technical): E3: no artifacts — no stray rectangles, debug marks, rendering glitches; any visible artifact is a deductible defect
How it helps automated designs: Catches invisible-in-source rendering artifacts (leftover debug shapes, PIL bounding boxes, CSS overflow boxes) that only appear in rendered output
Drawbacks: Subjective at the margin — a deliberately subtle design element could be misclassified
Plain-language explanation: If there is a mystery box, line, or smudge on the page that does not belong to the design, it is a defect

Name: Squint Test Hierarchy Gate
What it does (technical): Generate Gaussian-blurred PNG of each page (convert -blur 0x12); inspect whether the most important element still dominates; automatable as screenshot QA with vision LLM
How it helps automated designs: Catches density inversions (caption louder than title, footer chrome louder than content) that pixel-perfect checks report as ''fine''
Drawbacks: Subjective without a vision-LLM pairing; only catches hierarchy, not text errors
Plain-language explanation: Take your glasses off and squint — whatever you can still see is what the page is about

Name: Image Validation Quarantine
What it does (technical): validate-image.py runs magic-byte plus Pillow decode before any API call; invalid files moved to _quarantine/
How it helps automated designs: Downloaders silently save 404 HTML pages as .jpg; sending these to vision API returns sticky 400 that requires /clear — quarantine prevents the unrecoverable failure
Drawbacks: HEIC files skip Pillow check; corrupt HEIC can still reach API; quarantine move is || true
Plain-language explanation: Like a receiving dock that refuses to unload boxes that rattle wrong — never let bad input reach the expensive worker

Name: Variant Eyebrow Stamp
What it does (technical): Every variant slide carries a mandatory eyebrow label like ''V1 — DIRECTION NAME''; format ''V1 · EDITORIAL ATLAS''
How it helps automated designs: Prevents silent variant collapse — when three variants render and any two look similar, the user can still identify which code produced which slide
Drawbacks: Occupies top-left corner always; must be stripped when the chosen variant becomes the main build
Plain-language explanation: Like sticky-note labels on prototypes in a user-testing session — you want to know which is Prototype A before any discussion
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Structural Distinctness Mandate
What it does (technical): The 3 variants MUST be structurally distinct — not three color palettes of the same layout. Scaffold provides three separate top-level functions (variant_v1, variant_v2, variant_v3) each building from a blank slide
How it helps automated designs: Forces compositional divergence rather than parameter-tweak divergence; a model without this produces same-grid different-colors variants
Drawbacks: Harder to implement; each variant requires full slide-composition code; build time roughly 3× a shared function
Plain-language explanation: Asking a chef for three different dinners — pasta, curry, sandwich are different meals, not the same pasta in three sauce colors

Name: Three-Axis Direction Spread
What it does (technical): One conservative variant (Upgraded Rhythm, Tinted Paper); one structural (Two-Panel, Editorial Atlas, Band); one dramatic (Hero Quote Split, Cinematic Canvas, Photo-Break)
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the model from clustering proposals around the path of least resistance — three different compositional axes guarantee real range
Drawbacks: Dramatic direction sometimes rejected as too radical; some deliverables (no imagery, dense tables) make dramatic unusable
Plain-language explanation: A real estate agent showing one starter home, one mid-range, and one aspirational — not three mid-range houses with different carpet
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Three-Variant Anti-Paralysis Cap
What it does (technical): 3 is the sweet spot — more invites paralysis, fewer doesn't show range; allow 4 implicitly as blends but default to 3
How it helps automated designs: Keeps the decision space human-sized; prevents hedging by producing many similar options
Drawbacks: 3 is social convention, not mathematical optimum; some decisions genuinely benefit from 4
Plain-language explanation: A car rental counter offering compact, midsize, full-size — not eight variants of midsize

Name: Named Compositional Directions
What it does (technical): 10-entry catalog: Editorial Atlas, Cinematic Canvas, Hero Quote Split, Data-Dominant Strip, Band Composition, Upgraded Rhythm, Tinted Paper, Two-Panel Spread, Photo-Break, Diptych — each with canonical layout spec
How it helps automated designs: Replaces vague aesthetic prompting (''make it more editorial'') with precise compositional contracts — the model implements a spec rather than inventing one
Drawbacks: Catalog is finite; unique content types may not fit any direction cleanly
Plain-language explanation: A design firm's pattern library — instead of describing ''something dramatic'' you say ''Cinematic Canvas'' and everyone knows the exact overlay opacity

Name: Scratch Deliverable Isolation
What it does (technical): Variants always build into a separate variants.pptx in the same directory; the main build is only modified after the user explicitly selects a variant
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates the most common failure mode of iterative visual refinement: accidentally corrupting the main deliverable mid-exploration
Drawbacks: Requires duplicating or importing the main build's design constants; constants can drift
Plain-language explanation: Sketching on tracing paper laid over a technical drawing — the original is never touched until the sketch is approved

Name: Diagnostic Language Gate
What it does (technical): Phase 1: 'data cards feel isolated because there's no visual connection to the narrative above,' not 'this looks bad'; surface 3-5 observable problems; if nothing concrete, ASK the user
How it helps automated designs: Prevents manufactured criticism — a model without this gate invents problems to justify exploration, biasing variant direction toward solving non-problems
Drawbacks: Requires genuine visual comprehension of the screenshot; if screenshot read fails, model may still invent
Plain-language explanation: A doctor describing symptoms precisely (''the joint shows fluid accumulation'') before ordering tests — not ''your shoulder looks bad''

Name: Surgical Iteration Lock
What it does (technical): For each issue, make a single targeted edit and re-render; do NOT redesign; after 3 cycles without convergence stop and ask the user
How it helps automated designs: Breaks the failure mode where integration issues become a license to redesign and scope creeps each iteration
Drawbacks: 3-cycle ceiling can be tight for complex integration issues (font fallback differences)
Plain-language explanation: A surgeon who fixes exactly the identified pathology and closes — not exploring adjacent tissue while in there

Name: Three-Tier Token Resolution
What it does (technical): Token order: medium constraints → theme → component token → core token → palette; QA test CLR-01: all color values reference tokens, not raw hex
How it helps automated designs: Prevents agents from inventing one-off values; consistency emerges structurally, not from agent diligence
Drawbacks: Authoring overhead; deep chains obscure which palette swatch a component actually resolves to
Plain-language explanation: Like a building code that says ''use the approved load table'' rather than ''guess the weight''
Source: Inside: design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Personality Tokens Numeric Axes
What it does (technical): Five numeric scores: warmth, playfulness, energy, formality, density (each 0-10); modulate token selection across all design categories simultaneously
How it helps automated designs: Anchors all local decisions to a single aesthetic register — without it agents make locally correct but globally inconsistent choices
Drawbacks: Score-to-token mapping is guidance, not formula; 0-10 scale is coarse
Plain-language explanation: A character sheet in a tabletop RPG — a warmth score of 7 tells every player how the character reacts without scripting every scene
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Personality-Toggle As First-Class Pattern
What it does (technical): Density toggle simultaneously changes 4 linked properties: component size tier, spacing scale, type tokens, grid mode — a documented pattern with defined scope, not a theme variant
How it helps automated designs: One system with a documented toggle covers both density tiers — no parallel artifacts
Drawbacks: True toggle requires all 4 changes driven by one CSS class — spec describes but doesn't code
Plain-language explanation: Like an aircraft cockpit ''day/night'' display mode — one switch dims every instrument together
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge + outside research

Name: Invariants Vs Variation Axes
What it does (technical): Two explicit sections: invariants (contrast ratios, base unit, typeface family, logo proportions) vs variation axes (hue rotation, corner radius, illustration pose)
How it helps automated designs: Prevents generative agents from varying brand-breaking properties AND from fixing properties that should vary
Drawbacks: Identifying invariants requires predicting identity-breaking violations — judgement call
Plain-language explanation: Like a jazz standard — chord changes are invariant, melody is variation

Name: Seeded Reproducible Imperfection
What it does (technical): Given the same seed or input, the same imperfection appears; variation ranges specified (stroke-width ±0.3px, card rotation ±0.5deg) but resolve deterministically
How it helps automated designs: Stable analog aesthetic across renders; enables visual regression testing and client/server consistency
Drawbacks: Spec requires seed but doesn't specify derivation (element ID? DOM position? explicit param?)
Plain-language explanation: A casting mold — each piece feels unique, but pieces from the same mold are identical

Name: Contextual Override Priority
What it does (technical): Fixed precedence: user preference > locale/a11y > content-type > user-role > viewport > data-volume > time > default; same-priority: later-defined wins
How it helps automated designs: Deterministic conflict resolution when multiple adaptive rules apply simultaneously
Drawbacks: Later-defined-wins is brittle (YAML order shouldn't dictate); user preference at top can override a11y
Plain-language explanation: Like a legal hierarchy — federal > state > local; when rules conflict you always know which wins

Name: Reduced-Motion First-Class
What it does (technical): Required reduced_motion_policy field per animation: 3 acceptable strategies — disable, opacity-only, instant; ''reduce but slow down'' explicitly prohibited
How it helps automated designs: Reduced-motion becomes part of the spec, not a CSS afterthought; closes the ''slower = less motion'' mistake
Drawbacks: Three strategies don't cover loading spinners that must remain visible
Plain-language explanation: Like a restaurant that designs the vegetarian menu at the same time as the regular menu — not as a single sad afterthought.

Name: Influence Traceability Gate
What it does (technical): Phase 5 self-validation: each influence has ≥2 specific Phase 1 observations supporting it; otherwise removed or merged
How it helps automated designs: Prevents hallucinated influences (''Müller-Brockmann for any grid design'') and keeps dossier tethered to sample
Drawbacks: Low bar for strong claims; some subtle real influences may show in only one observation
Plain-language explanation: A detective rule — you can't name a suspect without at least two pieces of evidence

Name: Critical-Failure Score Cap
What it does (technical): Any failed critical test caps the maximum score at 0.70 — applied before weighted score
How it helps automated designs: Accessibility / structural failures become non-maskable — can't produce a beautiful doc that fails WCAG contrast
Drawbacks: Uniform cap regardless of which critical test failed; may incentivize ''pass the test'' over genuine quality
Plain-language explanation: Like a car inspection that fails the entire vehicle if the brakes don't work — no partial credit on safety
Source: Inside: brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Frozen Hermetic Token Dict
What it does (technical): All design tokens inlined as Python dicts with token_hash comment — hermetic between MCP fetches; same YAML always produces same HTML regardless of MCP availability
How it helps automated designs: Reproducible builds across MCP server state; manifest hash documents provenance
Drawbacks: Tokens go stale silently if design system updates; drift invisible until visual regression
Plain-language explanation: Like printing a brand style guide into every employee handbook rather than linking to the live intranet — always available, possibly out of date

Name: Variant Token Inheritance
What it does (technical): Variant tokens are shallow copies overriding only differing keys: T_STILLNESS = { **T_RIDGELINE, ''variant'': ''stillness'', ''display_family'': ... }
How it helps automated designs: Every color token, grid constant, and type scale inherited verbatim; guarantees cross-variant visual consistency on all non-display elements
Drawbacks: Dict spread is shallow — any future mutable value added to base would be shared across variants
Plain-language explanation: Like a CSS :root variable override — the child theme declares only what it changes; everything else inherits
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Editorial Cascade Override
What it does (technical): Variant-specific overrides applied via single trailing cascade block: append a CSS block at the end of <style> that wins all earlier rules
How it helps automated designs: Rather than branching through every CSS rule, one final block blanket-applies the variant — appears last and wins the cascade
Drawbacks: Override is coarse — all listed elements get the same treatment with no per-element exception
Plain-language explanation: Like a final ''house style'' memo that overrides every earlier instruction — one block at the end changes everything without rewriting the rules
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: Minimal-Weights Font Loading
What it does (technical): --minimal-weights flag collapses 9-stop weight palette to {300, 400, 600} and rewrites the Google Fonts URL to load only those three weights
How it helps automated designs: Reduces HTTP payload and font-load time — V1 ships faster without losing the core weight contrasts
Drawbacks: Subtle weight gradations (e.g., 650 for table footers) snap to 600 with noticeable change
Plain-language explanation: Like telling a print shop to stock only three ink densities instead of ten — still prints, but subtle gradations are lost

Name: Hash-Keyed Atomic Manifest
What it does (technical): Brand manifest co-located with assets at {asset_dir}/.acos-ultimate-designer-manifest.yaml, keyed by sha256, atomic write via .tmp → rename
How it helps automated designs: sha256 key makes re-scans idempotent (only new/changed files trigger re-analysis); atomic write makes parallel runs safe
Drawbacks: Manifest stale if user renames/moves files; hidden file easy to accidentally delete
Plain-language explanation: Like a library card catalog in the same room as the books — move the collection, the index travels with it

Name: Explicit Background Inheritance Chain
What it does (technical): section, article, header, footer, .card, .box, .panel { background-color: inherit } plus mandatory explicit background-color on every container element
How it helps automated designs: Headless Chromium doesn't paint transparent backgrounds in print — transparent renders as white and bleeds through dark-paneled pages; the chain ensures dark colors propagate
Drawbacks: Every div carries a redundant inline background-color; a missed element causes a visible artifact
Plain-language explanation: Like requiring every actor on a dark stage to explicitly wear dark clothing — no one relies on stage lights handling their transparency
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Hardcoded Hex In Hero Footer
What it does (technical): No CSS var() references in hero or footer background-color declarations — use literal hex (#465D53) not var(--sage-80) in structural elements
How it helps automated designs: PDF and mobile artifact renderers may fail to resolve CSS variables before painting — hardcoded hex eliminates that failure mode for critical surfaces
Drawbacks: Brand color change now requires updating both var() definition AND each hardcoded instance — slightly less maintainable
Plain-language explanation: Like writing ''three hundred and forty-two dollars'' in full on a check rather than just the numerals — redundant, but survives parsing

Name: LaTeX Float Placement
What it does (technical): LaTeX [htbp] global float optimization; CSS Paged Media float: top/float: bottom (WeasyPrint/Prince); Typst figure(placement: auto) — engine picks page placement
How it helps automated designs: When auto-generating multi-page PDFs with figures, you don't know which figure lands which page — the engine picks
Drawbacks: Famously surprising — [h] rejected because rag is bad; figures drift far from reference
Plain-language explanation: Hand the engraver photos with ''stick each one where it looks nice, in this preference order'' instead of nailing each to a fixed page
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants + outside research

Name: H&J As Named Style Bundles
What it does (technical): H&J (Quark/InDesign) is a named bundle of hyphenation + justification specs; modern: CSS custom properties + design tokens (Style Dictionary)
How it helps automated designs: Naming the H&J bundle and inheriting through paragraph styles was the original design token pattern — 25 years before the term
Drawbacks: Inheritance order surprises (app default → project → style sheet → local)
Plain-language explanation: Teach the cook ''Tuscan seasoning'' once instead of dictating salt/pepper/oregano amounts every time

Name: Document Class As Cohesive Design
What it does (technical): LaTeX document classes (article, book, report) encapsulate page geometry + sectioning + default fonts + figure behaviors + bibliography as ONE decision
How it helps automated designs: Modern auto-gen fragments this — one class equals one cohesive design, not a hundred independent knobs
Drawbacks: Class lock-in — switching article → book mid-project breaks everything
Plain-language explanation: A pre-set oven program (Bread/Roast/Pizza) — one button, not eight dials

Name: Variable Fonts Optical-Size Axis
What it does (technical): OpenType Variable Fonts (2016) with weight/width/opsz axes; CSS font-variation-settings — body at 9pt slightly heavier opsz than same family at 36pt headline
How it helps automated designs: For density-controlled deliverables, optical-size axis is the biggest readability win — type adjusts stroke contrast to size
Drawbacks: Knuth's lesson — exposing 60 parameters is impossible; variable fonts succeed because they expose 2-4 axes
Plain-language explanation: Instead of 12 cans of ''boldness paint,'' one dial from light to black, mixing in real time
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, forge + outside research

Name: Semantic AST Bridge
What it does (technical): Maintain one semantic AST (Pandoc, MDX, Hugo goldmark); render to many physical formats — AST stores ''section heading level 2,'' not ''18pt bold''
How it helps automated designs: Pipelines generating markdown → both PDF and PPTX should share AST stage, not re-render from rendered intermediate
Drawbacks: Lossy round-trips between formats; extensions create dialects
Plain-language explanation: Translate a novel via a detailed plot outline, not by re-translating from the previous translation

Name: Smart Text Reflow Pagination
What it does (technical): CSS Paged Media auto-pagination (WeasyPrint/Prince/paged.js); LaTeX inherently — pages appear/disappear as content grows
How it helps automated designs: Pipelines pre-computing ''this content needs N pages'' are brittle — content adds a paragraph and layout breaks. Threading is authoritative
Drawbacks: Page count becomes non-deterministic — bad for ''report must be exactly 40 pages'' contracts
Plain-language explanation: A spiral notebook that grows pages when you write too much — content drives count, not the other way around

Name: Right-Align Numbers Left-Align Text
What it does (technical): td.num { text-align: right } plus tnum equals de-facto decimal alignment; headers should align with their column
How it helps automated designs: Trivial dtype-based rule; numbers line up at decimal point, text reads from left
Drawbacks: Headers must align with their column type — easy to miss
Plain-language explanation: Numbers line up at the decimal point like soldiers; text reads from left like a sentence
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Units In Header Not Cells
What it does (technical): Header: ''Revenue (USD millions)''; cells: 42.1; auto-scale if max > 1e6 and stamp the unit in header
How it helps automated designs: ''No smoking'' sign at the entrance, not on every chair — saves rendering ''$'' forty times
Drawbacks: Mixed-currency tables can't use header-unit — need per-cell unit
Plain-language explanation: Put ''in dollars'' at the top of the column once, instead of writing ''$'' next to every number

Name: Light Zebra Striping
What it does (technical): tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #FAFAFA } — only when rows ≥ ~6, and 1-3% darker than white
How it helps automated designs: Row-count check applies single CSS class; faint stripes help with row tracking
Drawbacks: Tufte camp says no striping ever; NN/g research says light stripes help
Plain-language explanation: Faint stripes are bowling-alley lane lines — keep your eye on the row, whisper not shout

Name: No Bold Vertical Borders In Tables
What it does (technical): table { border-collapse: collapse } td, th { border: none; padding: 6px 12px } — horizontal rules only; whitespace separates columns
How it helps automated designs: One CSS rule replaces dozens of border declarations; padding does the work
Drawbacks: Long text in adjacent columns can visually merge — enforce ≥8px padding
Plain-language explanation: A table doesn't need a fence between every cell — padding separates columns like physical distance separates people in line

Name: Semibold Header With Bottom Rule
What it does (technical): thead th { font-weight: 600; border-bottom: 1px solid #333; padding-bottom: 6px } — no fill
How it helps automated designs: Single styled thead rule everywhere; clean professional header
Drawbacks: Brand kits may require fill — needs opt-out
Plain-language explanation: A header doesn't need to shout — a neat underline says ''this is the heading''
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Total Row With Double-Rule
What it does (technical): tr.total td { border-top: 1px solid #333; font-weight: 600 } and double-rule (border-top: 3px double) for grand totals — accounting convention
How it helps automated designs: Generator knows which row it summed; double-rule signals grand total per accounting convention
Drawbacks: Subtotal plus grand-total need their own hierarchy
Plain-language explanation: The total row is the ''bottom line'' — earns a horizontal rule above it like a check earns a signature line

Name: Table Footnotes Symbol-Anchored
What it does (technical): .t-note { font-size: 0.75rem; font-style: italic; color: #555; margin-top: 6px } with <sup>1</sup> anchors; use ¹²³ symbols not asterisks
How it helps automated designs: Footnotes templated as (value, note_id) tuples; structured, scannable, conventional
Drawbacks: Cap at 3 per table — more is unreadable
Plain-language explanation: Small print at the bottom of a contract — present, readable, quiet

Name: Sort By Significance
What it does (technical): df.sort_values(by=primary_metric, ascending=False); alphabetical only for lookups
How it helps automated designs: If title contains ''by [metric],'' sort by it descending; data answers ''who's biggest'' by row order
Drawbacks: Time-series must sort chronologically — needs override flag
Plain-language explanation: Alphabetical is for phone books — tables exist to answer ''who's biggest,'' so sort to the answer

Name: Auto-Numeric Cell Classification
What it does (technical): is_num(s) → True if s[0] in '$(' or s[0].isdigit() or s.endswith('%') or s.endswith('×'); right-align and apply tabular-nums automatically
How it helps automated designs: All table cells default to tabular numerals; Python auto-classifies cells by inspecting first or last character — no column declarations in YAML
Drawbacks: Heuristic misclassifies ''N/A'', ''TBD'', ''3 bedrooms''; mixed cells (''$57M (est.)'') only checked at first char
Plain-language explanation: A spreadsheet that auto-switches to accounting alignment when you type a dollar sign — numeric cells detected without explicit instruction

Name: Trailing-Empty Colspan
What it does (technical): _trailing_empty(row) counts blank cells at end; if last non-empty cell is followed by trailing empties, expand with colspan=''N+1''
How it helps automated designs: YAML authors get spanning label rows just by leaving trailing columns empty — implicit table layout intelligence
Drawbacks: Only trailing empties are spanned (interior empties render blank); behavior is opaque to YAML authors
Plain-language explanation: Like a word processor that merges cells when adjacent ones are left blank — the author gets a span by omitting trailing values

Name: Dollar Auto-Abbreviation
What it does (technical): $57,000,000 → $57.0M; $1,200,000,000 → $1.2B; regex requires the value to be purely a dollar literal — anything else passes through unchanged
How it helps automated designs: Raw dollar values from YAML automatically display-abbreviated in comparison cards and part-meta strips
Drawbacks: Regex requires pure dollar literal — trailing qualifier (''$57M*'') passes through; one-decimal shows .0 for round millions
Plain-language explanation: Like an Excel custom number format applied only to hero-number cells — a purpose-built formatter that activates in display contexts

Name: Photo-Slot Tag System
What it does (technical): HTML attributes data-photo-slot=''hero,landscape,architectural,cover'' plus data-slot-id matched against brand-asset manifest semantic_tags by fill-photo-slots.py
How it helps automated designs: Decouples layout authoring from image sourcing — a model generates a template specifying compositional intent without knowing the image file
Drawbacks: Tag vocabulary is informal — mismatched tags cause silent non-matches that fall through to the API or striped placeholder
Plain-language explanation: A magazine layout that marks each image frame with ''PHOTO: exterior shot of building at dusk'' — the photo editor fills it later
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Photo-Slot Missing Guard
What it does (technical): [data-photo-slot]:empty:not([style*=''background-image''])::before { content: ''IMAGE MISSING''; background: repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, #ffcccc, ...) }
How it helps automated designs: Self-documenting empty slots in QA without painting stripes over slots that already resolved
Drawbacks: Breaks if 'background-image :' (space before colon) is produced — silent
Plain-language explanation: A picture hook that only shows ''NO PHOTO'' when there's no picture — once you hang something, the label disappears
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Content-Shape Template Classification
What it does (technical): classify_section(): metrics list → metric-grid; steps → timeline; portfolio → portfolio-grid; items[{name, description}] → product-detail; default → two-column-narrative
How it helps automated designs: Users supply domain YAML, not template names — section with metrics: automatically becomes 3×3 KPI grid; zero template knowledge required
Drawbacks: First-match wins; combination sections forced into one template; heavy fallback to two-column-narrative produces visually repetitive documents
Plain-language explanation: A smart filing cabinet that reads the first line of each document and puts it in the right folder
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Risk-Item Auto-Detection
What it does (technical): Look for regex ^R\\d+\\s+[—-] in item names; if any item matches, switch the entire list from compact items-grid to full-width risk-grid layout
How it helps automated designs: Detection automatic from YAML naming convention; no separate schema flag
Drawbacks: Detection is list-wide — one matching item switches all items; mixed lists not supported
Plain-language explanation: Like a form that switches from single-line entries to paragraph boxes when it detects a long answer

Name: Roman-Numeral Page Numbering
What it does (technical): All pages including cover, dividers, photo-breaks receive Roman numerals; footer: {{page_number_roman}} / {{total_pages_roman}}
How it helps automated designs: Roman numerals signal ''designed object'' rather than utilitarian spreadsheet
Drawbacks: 40+ pages produce lengthy strings (''XLVII / CXII'') that overflow 11px footer cells
Plain-language explanation: Like Roman numerals in a book's front matter — signals a designed object rather than a spreadsheet printout

Name: Metric Card Coral Top-Border
What it does (technical): Each metric card: border-top: 3px solid var(--coral); hard-sliced to metrics[:9]; three-tier hierarchy mono-label (coral 11px caps) → display-data (48px Cormorant) → body-card-sm
How it helps automated designs: Coral top-border provides visual separation in 3×3 grid without shadows that fight warm background; hierarchy hardcoded so KPI data renders in correct order
Drawbacks: 10+ metrics silently dropped with no warning; long value strings overflow at 48px
Plain-language explanation: A scoreboard with 9 numbered slots — every stat gets identical treatment regardless of who is winning
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Photo-Break Terminal Flush
What it does (technical): After section loop, unconditionally append a photo-break page if content_pages_since_photo > 0; separate from in-loop every-3-pages insertion
How it helps automated designs: Documents whose section count isn't divisible by 3 would otherwise end with 1-2 content pages before closing — terminal flush ensures closing is always preceded by full-bleed photography
Drawbacks: Short documents may get two consecutive photo pages
Plain-language explanation: Like a magazine editor who always inserts a full-page photo before the back cover
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, design-variants, doc-design-qa, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Card Left-Border Accent
What it does (technical): .card { border-left: 3px solid #465D53 } — every card has a 3px sage left accent by default; on sage sections adapts to rgba(255,255,255,0.15)
How it helps automated designs: Gives each card a strong left-edge visual anchor mimicking editorial pull-quote conventions; cards feel framed and intentional rather than floating boxes
Drawbacks: No systematic rule for varying border color per card — leaves a decision point for the agent
Plain-language explanation: Like the colored tab on a file folder — every folder gets a tab automatically, telling you at a glance these are organized entries
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Authorship Attribution Block
What it does (technical): Hardcoded <div> below </footer> with inline style: background-color, padding, mono font, gray color, letter-spacing — containing author + lab + date
How it helps automated designs: Ensures every generated document carries an institutional attribution distinguishing it from anonymous AI output
Drawbacks: Date is hardcoded and goes stale; author hardcoded so unsuitable if skill is used by others; bypasses design token system
Plain-language explanation: Like a printer's colophon at the back of a book — a small but mandatory production credit signaling professional production

Name: Clamp() On Display Font Sizes
What it does (technical): All display fonts use clamp(): h1 hero font-size: clamp(42px, 6vw, 80px); section title clamp(32px, 4vw, 52px); fixed px only for body and data numbers
How it helps automated designs: Eliminates mobile overflow on large headlines automatically; agent uses display tokens without worrying about overflow at small viewports
Drawbacks: clamp() does not break words — a very long single word can still overflow at the minimum
Plain-language explanation: Auto-scaling text on a digital road sign — always fills available space up to a maximum but never shrinks below readable
Source: Inside: ascent-renderer, brad, doc-design-qa, forge, ultimate-designer + outside research

Name: Em-Dash En-Dash Hyphen Vocabulary
What it does (technical): em-dash (—, U+2014) for parenthetical breaks (Chicago: no surrounding spaces; Penguin/UK: hair-spaces); en-dash (–, U+2013) for ranges (1995–2010, pp. 23–47); hyphen (-, U+002D) for compound modifiers (loan-to-value, well-known). Auto-gen pipelines normalize via SmartyPants/typographer preprocessor since Markdown emits only `-` and `--`.
How it helps automated designs: Distinguishes thought-breaks from ranges from compounds — three different jobs, three different glyphs. A single correct em-dash signals competent typography; mixing them up signals machine output.
Drawbacks: Locale conventions vary (Chicago closed em-dash vs Penguin/Oxford spaced); Markdown source must be normalized at render time; old fonts may lack en-dash glyph and substitute hyphen silently.
Plain-language explanation: Three dashes that look almost identical do three different jobs — long for thought-breaks, medium for ranges, short for compound words.

Name: Locale-Aware Quote Marks
What it does (technical): Set quote glyphs per locale: English curly “” ‘’, German „“ ‚‘, French « » ‹ ›, CJK 「」『』. Drive via `<html lang="...">` plus SmartyPants/typographer pass; CSS `q { quotes: ... }` per language.
How it helps automated designs: Locale-correct quotes signal authored-not-generated output; reader trust climbs immediately on documents shipped into a localized market.
Drawbacks: Requires accurate lang attribute on every text root; code blocks and verbatim text must opt out (`<code>`, `<pre>`, `quotes: none`); machine translation often strips lang tags.
Plain-language explanation: Every language has its own way of dressing quotes — German uses low-9 marks, French uses arrowheads — and a renderer that doesn't notice looks foreign.

Name: Decimal-Place Discipline
What it does (technical): Match displayed precision to source precision; never render more decimals than the source carries. Conventions: currency 2 dp, percentages 1-2 dp, ratios 1-2 dp, basis points 0 dp, unit counts 0 dp. Round half-to-even (banker's) for financial reports.
How it helps automated designs: Prevents spurious-precision claims (4.327% when source said 4.3%); aligns auto-gen outputs with reconciliation-grade accounting practice.
Drawbacks: Inconsistent rounding across cells creates totals that don't tie; downstream Excel reconciliation breaks if some cells round and others truncate.
Plain-language explanation: If the source says 4.3% don't claim 4.327% — extra digits are unfunded confidence.

Name: Locale Number Formatting
What it does (technical): Comma vs dot decimal (1,234.56 US/UK vs 1.234,56 DE/IT); thousand separators (1 234 FR with non-breaking spaces U+00A0); negatives as parentheses (accounting) vs minus prefix (math/sci). Drive via `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, {...})` or locale-aware Jinja filter.
How it helps automated designs: One locale switch flips every number in the document to the audience's convention without per-cell edits; eliminates a major class of cross-border misreading.
Drawbacks: Mixing within a single document (1,234.56 next to 1.234,56) confuses every reader; CSV/XLSX exports must carry their own locale or break when reopened in another locale's Excel.
Plain-language explanation: Numbers are written differently in different countries — a German 1.234 means a thousand, not point-two-three-four — so pick a locale and stick to it.

Name: Currency Symbol Placement
What it does (technical): Pre-symbol no-space ($1,234.56) for USD/CAD/AUD/HKD; post-symbol with space (10 €, 1 234,56 €) for EUR in most EU locales; ISO 4217 three-letter code (USD 1,234.56) in international/multi-currency documents. Use non-breaking space between symbol/code and amount.
How it helps automated designs: Locale-correct currency formatting prevents '€10' from looking machine-translated in a French document; ISO codes prevent ambiguity between $ (USD vs CAD vs AUD vs MXN).
Drawbacks: Legacy fonts may lack € or ¥ glyphs and substitute boxes; mixed currencies in one table require either uniform ISO code or explicit per-row symbol — never silent mixing.
Plain-language explanation: Where the dollar sign sits depends on what country you're in — in front in America, after the number across most of Europe, and as a three-letter code in international finance.

Name: Footnote Symbol Hierarchy
What it does (technical): When numeric superscripts ¹²³ are unavailable or undesired (e.g. tables with numerals already), fall back to the classical sequence *, †, ‡, §, ¶, ‖, then doubled **, ††, ‡‡, §§. Reset numbering per page in books; continuous across whole document for articles/memos.
How it helps automated designs: Provides a deterministic non-numeric footnote system that doesn't collide with table data; works on engines that can't render Unicode superscripts.
Drawbacks: Cormorant Garamond and some display serifs lack ‡ and § glyphs and silently substitute; large numbers of footnotes per page exhaust the symbol set and force fallback to numbers anyway.
Plain-language explanation: When numbered footnotes don't fit a design, typographers fall back to a fixed sequence of marks — star, dagger, double-dagger, paragraph — like notes in a music piece.

Name: Border-Radius Convention
What it does (technical): Pick one radius token per design system: 0 for Swiss/modernist/editorial, 4px for IBM Carbon/business, 8px for friendly/consumer, 12-16px for playful, 9999px for pill buttons. Define `--radius` CSS custom property and reuse everywhere.
How it helps automated designs: One token controls the whole document's emotional register; mixing radii is the most common amateur tell. Auto-gen pipelines that read the token produce internally consistent output.
Drawbacks: Mixed radii in one composition (4px cards + 12px buttons) look unsettled; pill radius (9999px) breaks on tall containers; print engines may round-trip CSS through unsupported syntax.
Plain-language explanation: Sharp corners feel formal, rounded corners feel friendly — pick one mood and use it everywhere.

Name: Shadow/Elevation Tier System
What it does (technical): Material Design 6-tier elevation (0/1/2/3/4/6/8dp); each tier is a tuple of y-offset + blur + spread + alpha (e.g. dp=2 → 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.12) + 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.06)). Editorial print caps to ≤1 shadowed element per spread.
How it helps automated designs: Tiered shadow tokens communicate layering hierarchy at a glance; auto-gen reads the tier and renders the right shadow tuple without per-component design work.
Drawbacks: Shadows render poorly in print PDFs (banding, dot-gain artefacts) — substitute with tint-overlay or hairline rule for print outputs; over-shadowing flattens hierarchy.
Plain-language explanation: Each layer of paper above the desk catches more light — shadows tell you which thing is sitting on top of which.

Name: Logo Clear-Space Rule
What it does (technical): Reserve 0.5× to 1× of logo height as empty padding on all four sides; no other element (text, image, rule, edge of page) may enter that zone. Codified in brand guidelines via a measured 'X-unit' (often the height of the wordmark cap-height).
How it helps automated designs: Auto-layout engines that respect clear-space produce logos that always look brand-correct; eliminates the cramped-logo-against-margin amateur look.
Drawbacks: Narrow page margins (≤0.5in) leave no room to honor clear-space; long horizontal logos eat the line width; some brand systems use 2× clear-space which fights dense layouts.
Plain-language explanation: A logo needs personal space — keep other elements at least half its height away, like the elbow room between people in line.

Name: Logo Minimum-Size Floor
What it does (technical): Never render the logo below the brand's smallest tested size — typically 24-32px height for digital, 0.5in (~36pt) for print. Auto-gen must check pixel/inch dimensions and fall back to a monogram or favicon-style mark when below the floor.
How it helps automated designs: Prevents the logo from smudging into illegibility on thumbnails, footers, and slide chrome; the fallback monogram preserves brand presence at small sizes.
Drawbacks: Complex multi-color logos become illegible long before they hit the geometric floor; some brands lack a designed monogram fallback and must substitute uglier stand-ins.
Plain-language explanation: Below a certain size, your company's logo just looks like a smudge — set a minimum and substitute a simpler mark when there's no room.

Name: Heading Hierarchy Progression
