What it does (technical): Never skip heading levels (h2 → h4 with no intermediate h3); cap visible depth at h4 in body documents, h3 in slide bodies; document outline (HTML5 outline algorithm) must be tree-shaped without leaps. Lint via `outline-checker` or axe-core.
How it helps automated designs: Tree-shaped heading hierarchy is required for screen-reader navigation, table-of-contents generation, and PDF bookmark trees; auto-gen pipelines that respect it produce traversable documents for free.
Drawbacks: Dense technical content sometimes legitimately needs h5/h6 — collapse via `<details>/<summary>` blocks or reset depth at chapter boundaries; rigid enforcement breaks reference material.
Plain-language explanation: Headings are like file folder tabs — you can't have a sub-sub-folder without first having a sub-folder above it.

Name: Bullet Glyph Convention
What it does (technical): Primary: • (U+2022 bullet). Secondary/nested: – (U+2013 en-dash) or ◦ (U+25E6 white bullet). Tertiary: ▪ (U+25AA black small square). Never render `*` or `-` as user-visible glyphs — those are Markdown source only; the renderer must substitute proper Unicode bullets.
How it helps automated designs: Proper bullet glyphs signal designed output instead of raw Markdown leakage; one of the simplest single fixes that lifts auto-gen documents from draft to deliverable.
Drawbacks: Bullet character must visually match the body font's weight and color tint; some condensed fonts render U+2022 too small and need a sized `::marker` selector; nested bullets need padding-left tuning.
Plain-language explanation: Bullets in a finished document use proper round dots, not the asterisks you typed in Markdown — like swapping shorthand for handwriting before mailing.

Name: Hanging-Indent List Markers
What it does (technical): ul, ol { list-style-position: outside; padding-left: 1.5em; } — bullets hang into the gutter while body text aligns flush to a single optical axis. Pair with `::marker` color/size tuning for refined appearance.
How it helps automated designs: Outside markers create a single clean text axis even across multi-line bullets; auto-gen output reads as typeset rather than browser-default.
Drawbacks: Deep nesting (3+ levels) compounds the gutter and pushes text off the right edge; narrow columns (<28em) leave no room for the hang.
Plain-language explanation: A bullet should sit just outside the body text like a numbered tab on a binder — text below the bullet still lines up with the text above.

Name: Cover-Page Anatomy
What it does (technical): Six canonical slots: (1) client/recipient name, (2) document title, (3) subtitle or category, (4) prepared-by/firm + author, (5) date (full month name, no abbreviation: 'May 2026' not '5/26'), (6) confidentiality stamp + deal/project name. Optional 7th: logo lockup.
How it helps automated designs: Templated slot system means auto-gen produces covers that look hand-laid every time; missing slots are caught at validation, not at delivery.
Drawbacks: Missing slots (no client name, no date) look amateurish; extra slots (project number + version + revision + status) look cluttered — discipline is the design.
Plain-language explanation: Every formal document cover has the same six things in the same six spots — like the standard credits at the start of a movie.

Name: Confidentiality Running Header
What it does (technical): On every interior page (not the cover): `CONFIDENTIAL — Subject to NDA` or `PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL` set in small-caps or eyebrow style at the top-left or top-right. Implemented via `@page { @top-left { content: 'CONFIDENTIAL — Subject to NDA' } }` at 50% opacity in chrome color.
How it helps automated designs: Auto-renders the legal flag on every page without per-page authoring; deal documents leaving the firm always carry the right marker.
Drawbacks: Cluttered if combined with chapter eyebrow + page number in the same corner; Chromium ignores @top-* margin boxes (Prince/WeasyPrint/PagedJS only); too-loud opacity competes with content.
Plain-language explanation: Every interior page wears a quiet 'don't share this' badge at the top — like a building wristband, visible but not in your face.

Name: Diagonal Watermark Conventions
What it does (technical): DRAFT / CONFIDENTIAL / SAMPLE / PRELIMINARY: 45° rotation, large display weight (120-180pt typically), 6-10% opacity, centered on each page. Implement via fixed-position pseudo-element or @page background-image; never use rendered text behind content (selectable text leaks the stamp).
How it helps automated designs: Single CSS rule stamps every page; visible enough to read at arm's length, faint enough not to fight the content; legal-defensible 'this is not final' signal.
Drawbacks: Photo-heavy pages may swallow a 6% opacity stamp — bump to 10-12% for those spreads; selectable-text watermarks leak into copy-paste and search index; print engines vary on rotation handling.
Plain-language explanation: The big diagonal DRAFT stamp across every page is at 45 degrees and faint enough to read through — like watermarked paper held up to a light.

Name: TOC Depth Cap
What it does (technical): Default visible depth: h1 + h2 only. Include h3 when document length < 40 pages or section count < 20. Never show h4+ in the main TOC — use sub-TOCs at chapter starts (mini-TOC of that chapter's h3/h4) for navigation.
How it helps automated designs: Caps TOC growth so it remains a navigation aid instead of becoming a parallel document; auto-gen pipelines reading the depth-cap produce scannable TOCs without manual pruning.
Drawbacks: Reference material and legal documents legitimately need h3/h4 navigation; chapter-level sub-TOCs add authoring overhead; collapsible TOCs (PDF bookmarks) can carry the full depth even when print TOC is capped.
Plain-language explanation: A table of contents shows the chapters and the main sections — sub-sub-sections would make it longer than the document itself.

Name: Appendix Pagination
What it does (technical): Appendix pages number as A-1, A-2, B-1, B-2 with letter prefix and en-dash; numbering resets at each appendix. Implemented via CSS `counter-reset: appendix-page` + `content: counter(appendix, upper-alpha) '-' counter(appendix-page)` per @page rule, or per-appendix page-style in Prince/PagedJS.
How it helps automated designs: Adding or removing an appendix doesn't renumber the main body's page references; cross-references to 'A-3' stay stable across revisions; standard convention in legal exhibits and engineering reports.
Drawbacks: Cross-references (TOC, see-page-X) must use the prefixed form and update when appendix order changes; non-paged-media engines (Chromium headless) can't reset @page counters cleanly.
Plain-language explanation: Appendices get their own page-numbering — like 'Track A-1' on a vinyl record — so adding one doesn't renumber the whole document.

Name: Pull-Quote Typography
What it does (technical): Distinct from blockquote: 1.5-2× body size, display serif (Cormorant, Playfair) in italic or roman, color tinted to accent (often coral or sage), framed by a left rule or large open-quote glyph (U+201C set 2-3× quote size, color-tinted). May break the underlying column grid to span two columns.
How it helps automated designs: Pull-quotes auto-promote a key sentence into a visual anchor; readers scanning the document land on the quote and absorb the thesis even without reading the body.
Drawbacks: Overuse weakens the device — one pull-quote per 2-3 spreads max; pull-quotes that don't appear in the body text confuse readers (they should be lifted, not invented); grid-breaking pull-quotes require manual flow review.
Plain-language explanation: A pulled quote is louder than a regular blockquote — bigger, in italic, often with a colored stripe — like a poster pulled from the wall of an essay.

Name: Caption Typography
What it does (technical): figcaption, .caption { font-style: italic; font-size: 0.85em-0.875em; color: rgba(ink, 0.6); margin-top: 0.5em; max-width: same as figure }. Anchored to the figure's left edge; preferred max 2 lines; period-terminated only if a full sentence.
How it helps automated designs: Captions visually defer to the figure they describe; consistent caption styling across a document signals editorial discipline without per-caption tuning.
Drawbacks: Low contrast (60% ink) on warm-cream backgrounds can drift below WCAG 3:1 minimum for non-text — verify per palette; italic Cormorant at 0.85em becomes hard to read at distance.
Plain-language explanation: Captions whisper — italic, smaller, slightly faded — like the small print under a museum painting.

Name: Acronym First-Use Expansion
What it does (technical): First use: 'Special Purpose Entity (SPE)' — full term followed by acronym in parentheses; subsequent uses: bare acronym ('SPE'). For very long documents, reset at chapter boundary so a reader joining mid-document gets re-introduced. Track via glossary preprocessor or `<abbr title="...">` lint.
How it helps automated designs: Auto-gen pipelines that track first-use produce reader-friendly documents without authoring overhead; new readers aren't lost in a sea of acronyms; older readers aren't condescended to with re-expansions.
Drawbacks: Tracking first-use across multi-author or stitched-together documents requires a glossary pass; chapter-reset rule needs explicit chapter boundaries; some acronyms (PDF, USA) are common enough to never expand.
Plain-language explanation: First time you mention an acronym, spell it out and put the short form in parentheses — after that you can just use SPE.

Name: PDF/UA Tagged-Content Accessibility
What it does (technical): Emit PDF/UA-1 semantic structure tags (Document, Part, Sect, P, H1-H6, Figure, Table, TR, TH, TD, L, LI) so screen readers can navigate the document tree; alt-text required on every Figure; reading-order in the tag tree must match visual reading order. Validate with PAC 2024 or veraPDF.
How it helps automated designs: Tagged PDF is legally required for many institutional/government deliverables; a single render-time setting unlocks accessibility for a whole document; tagged structure also improves Acrobat's reflow and copy-paste.
Drawbacks: Puppeteer/Chromium `printToPDF` does NOT emit tags as of 2026 — needs Prince, PDFreactor, or post-processing via pdfua/cpdf; tag-tree validation has a learning curve; alt-text authoring takes time.
Plain-language explanation: A PDF can carry an invisible blueprint of its structure for screen readers — without it, the document is just a flat image to anyone who can't see it.

Name: Alt-Text Mandate
What it does (technical): Every meaningful figure carries an `alt` attribute (HTML) or `/Alt` entry (PDF/UA); decorative-only images use `alt=""` (empty string, not missing); never auto-generate alt from filename (`alt="IMG_4521.jpg"` is worse than nothing). Authoring guideline: one sentence answering 'what and why'.
How it helps automated designs: Single-pass alt-text authoring at slice time unlocks screen-reader access for the document's entire lifetime; required by WCAG 1.1.1 (Level A) and PDF/UA.
Drawbacks: Requires real authoring effort — filename or AI-generated alt is often misleading; complex charts need long descriptions (longdesc or sibling text) that alt can't carry; decorative-vs-meaningful classification is judgment-dependent.
Plain-language explanation: Every meaningful picture in the document needs a one-sentence description — what it shows and why it matters — so the reader who can't see it isn't lost.

Name: Logical-Properties For Bidi Support
What it does (technical): Replace physical CSS properties with logical equivalents: `margin-inline-start` over `margin-left`, `padding-block` over `padding-top`, `border-inline-end` over `border-right`, `inset-inline-start` over `left`. Logical properties auto-flip for RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) and vertical writing (CJK).
How it helps automated designs: One codebase serves LTR + RTL + vertical writing modes without per-locale stylesheets; auto-gen pipelines emitting logical properties can localize without re-render.
Drawbacks: Paged-media engine support varies (WeasyPrint 60+, Prince 15+); older Chromium versions need fallbacks; mixed physical+logical properties in the same file create LTR/RTL inconsistency that's hard to debug.
Plain-language explanation: Some languages read right-to-left — writing 'start' and 'end' instead of 'left' and 'right' lets one CSS file work for all of them.

Name: Citation Style Discipline
What it does (technical): Pick exactly one citation style per document and enforce mechanically: Chicago (footnotes, humanities), Bluebook (US legal — In re Marriage of X, 123 Cal. App. 4th 456 (2024)), APA (academic, in-text author-date), IFRS/SOX (finance — IAS 36.12). Implement via BibTeX/.bst, CSL XML, or Pandoc citation processor.
How it helps automated designs: One enforced style means every footnote, every reference, every cross-document quote ties out; auto-gen pipelines that pick a style produce publication-grade reference apparatus without manual editing.
Drawbacks: Mixing styles within one document (Chicago footnotes + APA in-text) looks unedited and is the #1 tell of stitched-together authorship; legal and academic audiences are intolerant of style violations.
Plain-language explanation: Pick one way to cite sources and stick with it — mixing styles in a finished document looks like the author lost focus.
